intuition.text: Many related messages become one, and only once the set is whole. If you think in folds, an aggregator is a reduce per key whose inputs arrive scattered among other keys' inputs, and which must decide for itself when its list has ended. Until then it holds what it has and says nothing; the message that completes a set runs the fold, sends the single result and lets the set go.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public execution guide. DotLn, the operator's platform for running AI agents on pieces of work it calls orders, has every finished order checked by three fresh, independent reviewers, and lets the order go on to its full validation run only after all three have reported. When several orders are reviewed at once, their reports can reach one place mixed together. Merging them into one result per order means naming three things: which order a report belongs to (the correlation), when an order has heard enough (the completion condition; the guide asks for all three reviewers, not the first two, and that choice is a product decision) and how the reports become one message (the aggregation). DotLn's architecture describes the same move for its background checks: a reducer that gathers their results either when all have answered or when a time limit passes, which are two different completion conditions.

example.name: Three reviewers' reports on two orders
example.description: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public execution guide, where every piece of work, called an order, is checked by three independent reviewers before it may go further. Here two such orders, {first} and {second}, are each reviewed by the same three reviewers: Criteria, who checks that the order's requirements hold; Design, who looks for a simpler build; and Consistency, who checks that the documents and records around the change are up to date. Each reviewer sends the Aggregator one report on each order, naming the order and how many findings (problems) it raised, over one channel the three share, so reports on the two orders arrive mixed. The Aggregator reads which order each report is about and keeps it in that order's set. A set is complete once it holds a report from all {reviewers} reviewers; in the next step the Aggregator sends it on to the Next phase as one message, with the findings added up, and forgets it. The set for {second} fills first, so it goes on first, although the first report to arrive was about {first}. The orders themselves never move: only reports about them do.

step0.title: Read which order a report is about
step0.text: Every report comes down the one shared channel, whichever order it is about. The Aggregator reads the order the report names, and that alone decides which set it joins: B, the first report on {second}, starts a new set instead of joining the set for {first}. This is the correlation.

step1.title: Keep it in that order's set
step1.text: The first report on an order starts that order's set, and later reports on the same order join it. The sets are kept apart, so a report on {second} can never fill a gap in the set for {first}.

step2.title: Check whether the set is complete
step2.text: After each report the Aggregator checks only that report's set: does it now hold a report from each of the {reviewers} reviewers? Until it does, the set waits and nothing is sent. This is the completion condition.

step3.title: Send the set on and forget it
step3.text: Once it sees a set complete, the Aggregator sends it on in the next step as one message, with the findings added up, and drops the set. That is why the set for {second}, which filled first, reaches the Next phase before the set for {first}, although the first report to arrive was about {first}. Adding up is this aggregator's way of combining; another might keep only the worst report, or all of them.

pseudocode.ordinary:
sets = an empty map from each order to the reports kept for it
on each report from the shared channel:
  order = the order the report names

  set = sets[order], or a new empty set kept there
  add the report to set

  if set holds fewer than three reports (one from each reviewer, if none sends two):
    stop here; the set waits for its next report

  in the next step, send the Next phase one message:
    the order, with the findings of every report in set added up
  remove sets[order]

item0.relevance: Apache Camel is an open-source Java integration framework whose routes are written in the vocabulary of these patterns. Its Aggregate page shows what a production aggregator has to make configurable once the three decisions are taken seriously.
item0.explanation: A required correlation expression computes each exchange's key, and exchanges with the same key are merged one at a time by a mandatory AggregationStrategy, which receives the result so far and the new arrival. Completion is mandatory and may combine several conditions, whichever fires first: a size, an inactivity timeout or a predicate completes a group, a fixed interval completes every current group at once, a batch consumer's option completes once its whole batch has been aggregated, and an external controller can complete one group or all of them; the inactivity timeout and the interval cannot be used together. Groups live in a MemoryAggregationRepository unless a persistent repository is plugged in, and closeCorrelationKeyOnCompletion makes a late exchange for a finished key fail with ClosedCorrelationKeyException instead of starting a new group.

item1.relevance: Spring Integration is the Spring portfolio's messaging framework: it implements these patterns as message handlers between channels inside a Spring application. Its aggregator gives each of the pattern's decisions its own strategy object.
item1.explanation: A CorrelationStrategy groups messages, by default on the CORRELATION_ID header; a ReleaseStrategy decides when a group may go, by default once as many messages as the SEQUENCE_SIZE header promises are present; a MessageGroupProcessor builds the output, by default a list of the payloads. Groups are kept in a MessageStore, which may be persistent. A group timeout forces a stalled group out, discarded or, with send-partial-result-on-expiry, released incomplete. After a normal release the group's metadata stays so that late messages for it go to the discard channel, and the page warns that this kept state can exhaust memory unless a MessageGroupStoreReaper clears it. A reactive variant, FluxAggregatorMessageHandler, is built on Project Reactor's groupBy and window operators.

item2.relevance: Apache NiFi is a dataflow system that moves FlowFiles between processors arranged on a canvas. MergeContent is its processor for combining many FlowFiles into one, and its documentation is frank about what holding them costs.
item2.explanation: In the Defragment strategy, FlowFiles with the same fragment.identifier attribute share a bin, fragment.index orders them and fragment.count says how many make the bin complete; if Max Bin Age passes before the count is reached, every FlowFile in the bin goes to the failure relationship instead of being merged. In the Bin-Packing strategy a Correlation Attribute Name groups like FlowFiles, minimum and maximum counts or sizes complete a bin, and the number of bins is capped: when a new bin is needed at the cap, the oldest bin is merged early to make room. The page advises setting Max Bin Age almost always, so that FlowFiles cannot stay stuck when the data stops.

limits.item0: A lost report holds its set for ever. If Consistency's report on {second} never arrives, that set keeps A and B and never completes: nothing about {second} reaches the Next phase, and nothing raises an error. Waiting for every reviewer needs a time limit for each set beside it. Here that limit should raise an alarm or ask the missing reviewer again, not send on a set with a review missing, which would let an order go further unchecked.
limits.item1: Counting reports is not the same as hearing from every reviewer. DotLn's guide has all three reviewers check again after a repair, so one reviewer can report twice on one order. This Aggregator counts to {reviewers}: if Criteria sends a second report on {first} before Design has reported, the set goes on with two Criteria reports and none from Design, and Design's report that follows reaches the Aggregator and vanishes. Make the condition name the reviewers, decide whether a later report replaces an earlier one, and keep a second round of reviews in a set of its own.
limits.item2: A finished set either leaves a trace or leaves late reports nowhere to go. In this RxJS reading groupBy keeps every order it has seen for as long as the channel is open, so its memory grows with the orders, and a late report on an order already sent on goes to a group nobody listens to. Camel can refuse such a report and Spring Integration sends it to a discard channel; in RxJS a duration selector on groupBy forgets a finished group, after which a late report starts a new set that will never complete by itself.
limits.item3: The sets are state. If the Aggregator restarts, every set it was holding is lost, and unless the reviewers report again, those orders wait for ever. A store that keeps the sets, such as Camel's aggregation repository or Spring Integration's message store, is the price of an aggregator that can be restarted.
limits.item4: The analogy breaks at the shared channel. In DotLn the agent working on an order starts its own three reviewers and waits for them, so it knows which order a report is about from whom it asked, and nothing has to sort a mixed stream. An aggregator earns its place where replies to many requests share one channel; where each requester can wait for its own replies, a forkJoin over them is simpler.

item0.why: Reach for Correlation Identifier when choosing what each report must carry to be sorted: here the order number, or an order with its round of review, so that a second round cannot join the first round's set.

item1.why: Choose a Resequencer when related messages should all pass through unchanged and in order, rather than become one message.

item2.why: A Splitter is the usual partner upstream: one that numbers its parts and says how many there are lets the completion condition be the count each message carries instead of a fixed three.

item3.why: Scatter-Gather is the whole round trip, sending one order to three reviewers and gathering their reports; read it when the sending out matters as much as the gathering this Aggregator does.

item4.why: Read the row on aggregator state, persistence, scaling and late arrivals when the questions are the ones the last limits raise: where the sets live, and what a late report means.

item5.why: Message Expiration supplies the time limit an aggregator that waits for every reviewer needs beside it, for a report or a set that has waited too long.

intuition.text: Instead of every pair of parties agreeing a format between them, all of them agree one, owned by none of them. Each party then keeps two translators, its own format into the shared one and back out, and knows nothing about anyone else's format. Every message is translated twice, once on the way in and once on the way out, and in exchange a party can join, leave or change its own format without touching anyone else's code. The shared form is a decision about meaning: whatever it has no place for does not survive the trip.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's interfaces document at its pinned commit: the editable views of a loadout behave like the parties to a canonical data model, translating to one shared form and never to each other. A loadout is a configuration that DotLn compiles into a program, and it can be edited in three views: as typed code, as a function table or as statechart JSON. No view is the master copy: each converts its own format into one normalised loadout graph and back, and the document requires that converting out and back in returns the normalised graph. The compiler builds from that graph, so a sample loadout gives the same program, with the same hash, from any of the three views; a view that cannot convert back, such as a narrative, is labelled lossy.

example.name: One loadout, three editable views
example.description: As an analogy, read against DotLn's interfaces document: a sample loadout is shown in {views}. The operator changes its objective in the function table, then reorders the table's rows, and finally a narrative view is attached that can only read. Every message passes through the Loadout graph channel in the shared, normalised form: the editing view's decoder translates it in, each other view's encoder translates it out, and the compiler builds from the graph itself.

parameters.views: the code view, the function table and the statechart view

step0.title: Agree one form that no view owns
step0.text: The shared form is the normalised loadout graph: keys in order, set-like collections sorted, and no view's name or formatting in it. It belongs to none of {views}, so none of them is the others' master.

step1.title: Give each view its own pair of translators
step1.text: Each view has a decoder from its format into the shared form and an encoder back out. These two are the only code that knows that view's format, and nothing joins two views directly.

step2.title: Translate twice on every trip
step2.text: An edit made in one view is decoded once into the graph, then encoded once for each other view. The compiler reads the graph itself, so what it builds does not depend on which view the edit came from.

step3.title: Lose what the shared form does not carry
step3.text: Anything the graph has no place for is dropped on the way in. Reordering the function table's rows leaves the graph, and so the program and its hash, as they were, and encoding the graph back gives the rows in the graph's order.

step4.title: Join with one pair, or one encoder
step4.text: A new participant writes its own encoder, and a decoder if its format can round-trip. A view with no decoder, such as a narrative, can only read: an edit made in it reaches no one, so it is labelled lossy.

pseudocode.ordinary:
shared form = the loadout graph, normalised:
  object keys in order, set-like collections sorted,
  no view's name or formatting

for each view in code DSL, function table, statechart JSON:
  decode: view text -> shared form
  encode: shared form -> view text
  (only these two know the view's format)

on an edit in one view:
  graph = normalise(decode(edit))
  for each other view: show encode(graph)
  compiler builds from graph alone

if the edit changes only what the shared form drops,
such as the order of the table's rows:
  graph is unchanged, so the program and hash are too
  encode(graph) shows the rows in the graph's order

to add a participant:
  write its encode, and its decode if it can round-trip
  without a decode it can only read, and is labelled lossy

item0.relevance: CloudEvents is a specification, owned by no vendor, of the common attributes an event should carry, written so that producers, consumers and the tooling between them stop re-learning each producer's own way of describing events. It is a shared format that every party maps to instead of to each other, applied to events.
item0.explanation: Version 1.0.2 fixes the context attributes every event must carry, id, source, specversion and type, and optional ones such as datacontenttype, dataschema, subject and time, with event formats such as JSON for writing an event as bytes. What it standardises is the description of the event, not its payload: the specification places no restriction on the data, which is domain-specific and labelled by datacontenttype and dataschema. So it is a canonical model of the envelope only; the body still needs a model the parties agree among themselves.

item2.title: DotLn · Interfaces, the isomorphic views
item2.supports: Three editable views of a loadout, the typed code DSL, the function table and the statechart JSON, are each a complete representation of one LoadoutGraphV1 with its own encode and decode and the law decode(encode(x)) = normalize(x). Normalisation orders keys and sorts set-like collections, function-table rows among them by kind and key, keeps an explicit pipeline's order and repeats, and includes no view formatting or name; the Seiri fixture's three views give one semantic hash; and views that cannot round-trip, such as narrative, are labelled lossy projections.

item3.title: DotLn · IR verification, lineage and compatibility
item3.supports: The platform provides a verifier over its canonical JSON IR; an outside rule source is not presumed to be canonical IR, and each proposed mapping into it is labelled exact, adapted, lossy, unmapped, blocked or unverified, as provisional vocabulary; unknown compatibility fails visibly rather than being inferred.

limits.item0: Until there are enough participants, the shared form costs more than it saves: the worked step at the start counts the translators both ways for this example's views and finds no saving, and every edit now pays two translations instead of one. Two parties that only ever talk to each other are better served by a direct Message Translator each way.
limits.item1: The shared form drops whatever it has no place for. Here the order of the function table's rows does not survive the trip, which is right only because nothing means anything by it; DotLn's normalisation keeps an explicit pipeline's order, repeats included, because there order changes the program. Designing the model is deciding, field by field, what counts as meaning, and every participant has to agree to the answer.
limits.item2: Every participant depends on the shared form, so changing it touches every translator at once. Give the form a version that each message carries, a Format Indicator, and let a reader that meets a version it does not know refuse visibly rather than guess, as DotLn's IR compatibility rules require of its artifacts.
limits.item3: A participant that cannot round-trip, such as the narrative here, can only read: it has an encoder and no decoder, and an edit made in it reaches no one. Label it lossy, as DotLn's interfaces document does, so nobody mistakes it for a view they can edit in.
limits.item4: Where the analogy breaks: DotLn's views do not send messages through a channel. The views and the compiler meet in function calls over one normalised value, so the canonical model there is that value's shape; the Loadout graph channel and the steps here are the messaging reading of it.

item0.why: Each participant's decoder and encoder is a Message Translator; with only two parties, one direct translator each way is simpler than a shared form.

item1.why: Read the costs row when deciding whether a shared form is worth it: double translation, agreeing a model, keeping it to the message body and letting it evolve.

item2.why: A Format Indicator is what lets the shared form change: each message says which version it is in, so a reader can map or refuse it.

item3.why: A Normalizer is the inbound half at a single receiver: when one kind of message arrives in several formats, it routes each to its own translator into the one form.

item4.why: A Message Bus is the structure a shared form usually serves: common channels, a common command set and an adapter for each system, so systems can come and go.

item5.why: A Shared Database is the choice when the parties can share storage rather than exchange messages: one schema and no translators, at the price of every party depending on that schema directly.

start.note: Nothing has moved yet: the graph holds g, and every view was written from it.

0.note: The operator changes the objective in the function table, which sends it, t, to the graph. Only the table’s decoder reads table rows: it turns t into a new g, and no other view ever sees the table’s format.

1.note: The graph sends g out through two encoders: to the code view as c and to the statechart view as s. Neither view can tell that the change began as a table row.

2.note: The graph sends g to the compiler, which builds the program from g and never from a view, so it does not matter which view the edit was made in.

3.note: The operator reorders the function table’s rows, and the table sends them, t, to the graph. The decoder sorts rows by kind and key, so g comes out exactly as it was: row order has no place in the shared form.

4.note: The graph sends g to the compiler again; the reorder never reached it.

5.note: The graph’s encoder writes g back into the table as t, and the operator’s reorder is gone: it did not survive the trip through the shared form, which is right only because row order means nothing here.

6.note: A narrative view is attached, and the graph’s encoder writes g into it as prose, n. There is no decoder from prose back to a graph, so nothing written in the narrative can reach the other views.

intuition.text: An application that was never built to send or receive messages still has a way in and a way out: an API it answers, tables it writes, a screen it draws. A channel adapter stands at that edge and speaks for the application on the channel. When a message arrives, it makes the call the application already understands; when the application answers, or fails, it publishes that as a message. Nothing inside the application changes and the application never sees the channel, so everything that knows both sides lives in the adapter, and replacing either side means rewriting the adapter alone.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn-Angular's events and state guide. The board page talks only in events on the app's one event stream, while the app's HTTP API answers GET requests for uifa-board-v1 and knows nothing of events. The guide traces the path from the board's page events through BoardStore to boardHttpEvents.load, BoardApi and HTTP, with withCommand publishing the load's success or failure. Read withCommand and BoardApi together as the adapter: the board reaches the API's document only through that adapter code, and the API is attached at its edge without any change inside it. And because, as the guide explains, the API's reply keeps the uifa-board-v1 shape, pointing the board at the real API instead of the mock is a configuration change and leaves the facade and rendering alone. The reading is this study's; the app does not call the arrangement a channel adapter.

example.name: The board loads its document through an adapter
example.description: As an analogy, read against DotLn-Angular's events and state guide: the Board and the Adapter talk over the app's event stream, and the Adapter and the HTTP API serving {route} talk over HTTP. The board publishes load; the adapter turns it into a GET, and turns the 200 reply into loadSuccess with the document, which the board keeps. The reader then refreshes, the API answers {failure}, and the adapter publishes loadFailure, which clears the board's document. Each step moves one message along one line.

step0.title: Listen on the channel for the application
step0.text: The adapter subscribes to the events the application should act on, here load. The application itself never subscribes; it would not know how. The adapter keeps the event it is serving until it has an answer for it.

step1.title: Turn the message into the application's own call
step1.text: It makes the call the application understands, GET {route} through BoardApi. Nothing in the request says event: to the API it is one more HTTP client.

step2.title: Turn the answer into a message
step2.text: When the reply arrives, the adapter publishes loadSuccess with the document on the channel. Whoever listens, here the board's reducer, learns of the answer only from that message.

step3.title: Turn a failure into a message too
step3.text: When the call fails, as it does with {failure}, the adapter publishes loadFailure with an app error. Without this the channel would never hear of the failure, and the board would wait for an answer that is not coming.

pseudocode.ordinary:
on each load event on the channel:
  (the application itself never listens)
  keep the event as the one being served

  reply = call the application: GET /uifa-board-v1
  (to the API this is an ordinary HTTP request)

  if the reply succeeds:
    publish loadSuccess(reply.document) on the channel
    forget the event being served

  if the call fails:
    error = describe it: network, timeout, HTTP or unknown
    publish loadFailure(error) on the channel
    forget the event being served

item0.relevance: Apache Camel is the Apache Software Foundation's open-source integration framework; its documentation has a page for this pattern saying how Camel provides it.
item0.explanation: Camel has no separate adapter construct, because every component is one: a component hides how it reaches an outside system behind an endpoint URI. The page's route consumes a Kafka topic and hands each record's payload to a method on a plain bean that contains no Camel code, and it shows the same wiring declared instead with a @Consume annotation on that method. In the first form the application's side stays an ordinary object that knows nothing of Kafka or Camel.

item1.relevance: Spring Integration is the Spring portfolio's messaging and integration framework; its reference guide gives channel adapters a chapter of their own and treats its transport modules, such as JMS, files, HTTP and mail, as adapters too.
item1.explanation: It separates the two directions. An inbound adapter calls a method on an ordinary object each time its poller fires, at a fixed rate or on a cron expression, and sends each non-null result to a channel as a message; an outbound adapter calls a method with the payload of each message sent to its channel. The chapter explains a polling default worth knowing: an inbound adapter takes one message per poll unless told otherwise, so a source method that never returns null cannot trap the poller in an endless loop.

item2.relevance: Debezium captures the changes made to databases; its connectors are most commonly deployed in Kafka Connect, as source connectors that send records into Kafka.
item2.explanation: It attaches the adapter at the data layer rather than at an API. Its MySQL connector reads the database's binlog through a client library and its PostgreSQL connector reads a logical replication stream, and by default each table's changes go to a Kafka topic named after the table. The connector learns of each change from the database's own log, not from any call the application makes.

limits.item0: An adapter can publish only what its layer offers. The board's API answers when it is asked and announces nothing, so a change on the server reaches the event stream only when something publishes load again: the board is as fresh as its last load. If listeners must hear changes as they happen, attach where changes are recorded, as change-data-capture tools do by reading a database's log, or poll on a schedule and accept the delay.
limits.item1: The adapter decides what overlapping messages do, and that decision can lose answers. The app's command feature runs each call through switchMap, so a load that arrives while an earlier call is in flight cancels the earlier one and only the newer reply is published. For a read like this one that is right; for a write it would drop the confirmation of a change the server may already have made. An adapter for writes needs a queue or an exclusive policy, and a way for the application to recognise a repeated request.
limits.item2: Nothing makes the call and the publish one step. If the adapter stops after the application has acted but before it publishes, the channel never hears of something that happened; if it retries blindly, the application may act twice. A read can shrug this off; a write needs the call and the publish bound into one transaction.
limits.item3: The adapter puts the application's own data shape on the channel: loadSuccess carries the uifa-board-v1 document as the API returns it, so every listener depends on that schema. A second source with a different shape needs a translator, or a shared model that every adapter publishes.
limits.item4: The analogy stretches in one place: the app's event stream lives inside one browser tab, with no queue, no durability and no other application on it, and the API was written for this board. The pattern's usual case is a separate application that predates the messaging system and cannot be changed.

item0.why: Reach for a gateway when your own code should send and receive through a domain method, such as loadBoard(), without touching the channel's API: a gateway lives inside the caller, where an adapter stands outside an application that cannot be changed.

item1.why: When what the adapter publishes is not the shape the listeners need, a translator after it changes the shape without teaching the adapter about every listener.

item2.why: When the other side is itself a messaging system, join the two channels with a bridge instead; an adapter joins a channel to an application.

item3.why: When several adapters feed one channel, a shared model that all of them publish keeps listeners from depending on each application's own schema.

item4.why: When the adapter writes, so that the call into the application and the publish on the channel must succeed or fail together.

intuition.text: A command message is a request written down and posted instead of phoned through. The sender puts the name of the work and everything the work needs into one message, leaves it on a channel and carries on; whichever receiver picks it up does the work. Because the request now exists apart from both of them, it can wait for a busy receiver and goes to exactly one of several. The cost is that the sender hears the outcome only in a later message, and a request posted twice may be carried out twice.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public domain model: once DotLn's kernel, the part that decides what happens next, has authorised an action, it issues it as a Command carrying a fixed id, and the part the model calls the dispatch port hands the work order to a command-line session; the port first acknowledges the dispatch with a receipt, and the session's result later comes back naming that id. Here the kernel asks for order 41 to be verified while both sessions are busy, so a work order handed to a role reads as a command meant for one holder. The operator's typed phrase resume: verify has the same shape at the human end, with one difference DotLn's execution guide spells out: the phrase alone starts the session's work, and the recorded state of the work, not the phrase, says which order. A command message would carry the order inside it.

example.name: Verifying order 41: one command, two sessions
example.description: As an analogy to DotLn's dispatch of a work order: the kernel sends command {commandId}, verify order {order}, onto the dispatch channel while Session A and Session B are both busy. When both are free the channel gives it to B alone. B is slow, so the kernel's wait runs out and it sends {commandId} again; A takes the copy and verifies order {order} a second time. Both results reach the event store, each naming {commandId}.

step0.title: Write the work into the message
step0.text: The sender puts the procedure, verify, and its argument, order {order}, into one message with an id, {commandId}. Everything the receiver needs travels inside, so the receiver need not ask the sender or read shared state to know what to do.

step1.title: Post it and carry on
step1.text: The sender puts the command on a point-to-point channel and does not wait. If no receiver is free, the channel keeps the command; a direct call would have failed instead.

step2.title: One receiver takes it
step2.text: Of the receivers listening, the channel hands the command to exactly one, and the others never see it. That receiver runs the named procedure with the arguments in the message.

step3.title: Answer in a message of its own
step3.text: The outcome comes back as a separate message naming {commandId}, so the sender can match it to its request. Until it arrives the sender knows nothing about whether the work ran.

step4.title: A repeat is new work to the channel
step4.text: If the sender's wait runs out and it sends {commandId} again, the channel hands the copy to whichever receiver is free, and the procedure runs a second time. Only a receiver that checks the id against work already done can refuse it.

pseudocode.ordinary:
command = { procedure: verify, order, id }
  (everything the work needs is inside the message)

put command on the dispatch channel
carry on without waiting
  (while every session is busy, the channel keeps the command)

when a session is free and the channel holds a command:
  take it; no other session receives this one
  run command.procedure for command.order

send { answers: command.id, outcome } to the event store

if no answer naming command.id arrives within the wait:
  put command on the dispatch channel again
  (the next free session runs it again unless it first
   checks command.id against the work already done)

item0.relevance: Spring Integration is the Spring project for message-based integration in Java, and its reference names the integration patterns book as the source of its control bus. It has no page called Command Message; the control bus is where a message becomes a call to a named operation, the pattern at work inside one application.
item0.explanation: A message on the control bus's input channel names the operation in its payload as beanName.methodName and carries any arguments as a list in the CONTROL_BUS_ARGUMENTS header, which the page likens to binding a prepared statement's parameters. A registry resolves the bean and the method, and only eligible methods can be called: managed attributes and operations, lifecycle methods and some executor and scheduler settings. A return value can travel on through an output channel, and the page advises securing the input channel, since such messages can change the running system.

item1.relevance: NServiceBus is Particular Software's service bus for .NET. It treats command and event as two kinds of message type and checks the difference when the application runs, so it shows what the distinction buys once a framework enforces it.
item1.explanation: A command asks a service to do something and is sent to the one logical endpoint that owns it, where a single handler or saga deals with it; its name puts the verb first, as SubmitOrder does. Publishing a command, or subscribing to or unsubscribing from one, throws an exception unless that checking has been switched off, and the page counts a reply as neither a command nor an event.

item0.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns · Command Message
item0.supports: The catalogue places Command Message under Message Construction, treats it as an ordinary message that happens to hold a command rather than a special message type, gives a SOAP request as one, and relates it to Remote Procedure Invocation and Point-to-Point Channel.

item1.title: Hohpe and Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns (Addison-Wesley, 2003), Chapter 5: Message Construction, Command Message
item1.supports: The book covers the pattern in Chapter 5, Message Construction, in the section Command Message.

item2.title: DotLn product documents · 02 Domain model, at commit 9139d91
item2.supports: DotLn's domain model defines a Command as an authorised effect sent to an adapter, with a stable commandId the kernel computes and duplicate delivery ignored deterministically; records the adapter's result as a CommandResult event matched on that id and the transport's acknowledgement as a CommandReceipt; and names the work-order transport the dispatch port, whose request carries the persisted command and the compiled work order to a Claude or Codex command-line session.

item3.title: DotLn product documents · 07 Execution guide, at commit 9139d91
item3.supports: DotLn's execution guide says the operator's resume: phrase is the session's whole dispatch, with the durable control state rather than the phrase answering which work order, and that a driven phase interrupted part way receives the same phrase and briefing in a fresh session.

limits.item0: Posting twice means running twice. In the drawing the kernel cannot tell a slow session from a lost command, sends {commandId} again, and Session A verifies order {order} a second time: a point-to-point channel promises one taker per message, not per request. Give every command an id and have the receiver check it against finished work before acting, as an Idempotent Receiver does. DotLn's domain model says a duplicate delivery of a command is ignored by its stable id, and its execution guide hands an interrupted phase the same phrase in a fresh session, which is where such a check earns its keep. With competing receivers the record of finished ids has to be shared: Session A never saw the first delivery, so a memory kept by each session would not have stopped it.
limits.item1: A command fixes what happens next. The sender has to know the procedure's name and arguments, and every further reaction to the same change needs another command from it. When the sender should only report what happened and leave others to decide, an Event Message is the better fit.
limits.item2: Sent on a publish-subscribe channel, a command runs once per subscriber. It belongs on a point-to-point channel; NServiceBus, for one, throws an exception rather than publish a command.
limits.item3: The outcome is another message. Until a result naming {commandId} arrives, the sender cannot tell whether the work ran, failed or never started, so it needs a reply channel, an id to match on and a deadline, which is Request-Reply with a correlation identifier. When the caller cannot go on without the answer and the receiver is always up, a plain call is simpler than a command and its reply.
limits.item4: The analogy bends twice. DotLn's dispatch port launches the one session it hands the work order to, so no second session competes for it; the pair of sessions is the pattern's usual form, not DotLn's. And the operator's resume: phrase names only the procedure: if the control state changes between the phrase and the session reading it, the session acts on another order than the one meant, which a command carrying its own arguments avoids.

item0.why: Reach for an event message when the sender should report what happened and leave each receiver to decide, instead of ordering one receiver to act.

item1.why: Reach for a document message when the point is the data itself, such as a finished verification report, and the receiver chooses what to do with it.

item2.why: Remote Procedure Invocation is the simpler choice when the caller needs the answer before it can go on and the receiver is reliably there to give it.

item3.why: The point-to-point channel is what gives a command to exactly one receiver; read it for how that channel behaves on its own.

item4.why: Request-Reply is how the result finds its way back to the sender and is matched to the command that asked for it.

item5.why: An idempotent receiver is the remedy for the repeated command in the drawing: it recognises an id it has already handled and does nothing the second time.

start.note: Nothing has moved yet, and neither session is free to take new work.

0.note: The kernel sends command 7, verify order 41, to the dispatch channel, and goes on with other work instead of waiting for an answer.

1.note: Both sessions finish their earlier orders and start listening. Command 7 has waited in the channel for them; a direct call at step 1 would have found nobody free to answer.

2.note: The dispatch channel gives command 7 to Session B and to nobody else. Session A, just as free, gets nothing: a command is meant to be carried out once.

3.note: Session B is slow. The kernel’s wait for an answer to 7 runs out, and from where it stands a slow session and a lost command look the same.

4.note: So the kernel sends command 7 to the dispatch channel again. The copy is the same message as before, and the channel cannot tell it from new work.

5.note: The dispatch channel gives the copy to Session A. Order 41 is now being verified in both sessions for a single request.

6.note: Session B sends its result, b, to the event store. It names command 7, so it can be matched to the request that asked for it.

7.note: Session A sends its result, a, to the event store, also naming 7. The id shows that both answer one request, so a reader can keep one, but nothing undoes the second verification.

Dispatch, the pipe with the bold name, is the channel the pattern relies on: a command waits there until one session takes it. Session A and Session B are the two sessions that can carry a command out, and the Event store keeps their results. A token is a message: 7 is command 7, verify order 41, and b and a are the results that Session B and Session A send back. A token is green while it moves and outlined inside the box that holds it; a box a message leaves or reaches is outlined in green, and the words inside each box say what it is doing. intuition.text: A queue read by several sessions shares its work out instead of copying it. An order waits in the queue until some session is free, and that session alone receives it. Which session that is depends on who is free at the moment of handing out, not on whose turn it is: a session that finishes a short order comes back before one still busy with a long one, and an order that finds every session busy simply waits.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public execution guide. DotLn is the operator's agentic platform, where agent sessions take roles such as planning and execution on work orders. The guide runs several work orders side by side, each in its own worktree, a separate checkout of the repository, and lets only one session at a time write in a worktree: when two sessions race to take over a worktree whose writer has died, only one of them becomes its writer. Picture instead the planner, the role that files work orders, sending its orders into one Order queue and three agent sessions drawing from it, so each order is worked by exactly one session and an order that arrives while all three are busy waits for the first to finish. The Publish-Subscribe Channel study sends the same orders to the same sessions over a topic, where every session hears every order.

example.name: Four orders shared by three sessions
example.description: The planner sends orders {orders} to the Order queue at frames 1, 3, 5 and 7: the same orders, at the same frames, to the same three sessions as in the Publish-Subscribe Channel study. The queue has {consumers} consumers, Sessions 1, 2 and 3, all listening from frame 0, and can hand an order out from the frame after it arrives. Working orders 31, 32, 33 and 34 takes {work} frames respectively, and a session is free again the moment its work completes.

step0.title: Queue each order
step0.text: The planner sends an order to the queue and carries on. It neither waits for a session nor knows which one will take the order; the order joins the back of the queue.

step1.title: Line up the free sessions
step1.text: A session is free when it starts listening and again each time it finishes an order. Free sessions wait for work in the order they became free.

step2.title: Hand the oldest order to the first free session
step2.text: Whenever an order is waiting and a session is free, the queue takes the oldest order off and gives it to the session that has been free longest. The order leaves the queue as it is handed over, so no other session can receive it. With no session free, orders wait; with no order waiting, sessions wait.

step3.title: Work alone, then come back
step3.text: The session works on its order without telling the others. When the work is done it rejoins the line of free sessions, and may be handed the next waiting order at once, as Session 2 is given order 34.

pseudocode.ordinary:
when the planner sends an order:
  put it at the back of the queue
  hand out work

when a session starts listening, or finishes its order:
  put it at the back of the line of free sessions
  hand out work

hand out work:
  while an order is waiting and a session is free:
    take the oldest order off the queue
    give it to the session that has been free longest
    (the order is no longer in the queue for anyone else)

when a session is given an order:
  work on it, telling no other session
  when the work is done, the session has finished its order

item0.relevance: Apache Camel is the Apache Software Foundation's open-source integration framework, and its documentation describes how Camel expresses many of the book's patterns, this one among them. Its page for this pattern is read here at the 4.22.x long-term-support release.
item0.explanation: Camel takes the pattern from components that can consume concurrently, naming SEDA, JMS, Kafka and AWS components: on a JMS endpoint the concurrentConsumers option sets how many consumers read one queue, five in its example. For a component that cannot consume concurrently, the page shows one consumer handing each message to a pool of threads with the Threads EIP, which it calls a simulation of competing consumers. In its file example the pooled thread, not the polling one, moves a file to the backup folder once the file is processed, so a file that fails is not moved too early.

item1.relevance: Spring Integration is the Spring project's implementation of the book's messaging model inside a Spring application. Its page of channel implementations does not name this pattern, but its point-to-point channels are how several consumers share one channel's messages there.
item1.explanation: A QueueChannel wraps a queue with point-to-point semantics: however many consumers read the channel, each message is meant for just one of them. A send returns at once while the queue has room, even with no receiver ready, and blocks once it is full; a receive on an empty queue waits for a message or a timeout. A DirectChannel, also point-to-point, instead calls one of its subscribed handlers in the sender's own thread, chosen by a load-balancing strategy whose built-in option is round-robin, and falls over to the next handler when one throws.

item2.relevance: RabbitMQ is an open-source message broker. The second of its getting-started tutorials builds a work queue that distributes time-consuming tasks among several workers.
item2.explanation: Out of the box RabbitMQ deals messages to its consumers in rotation, round-robin, as they enter the queue and without looking at how many each consumer has yet to acknowledge; with two workers and alternating heavy and light tasks, one stays busy while the other idles. A prefetch of one stops it giving a worker a new message until that worker has acknowledged its last, so the next message goes to a worker that is not busy. With manual acknowledgement, a message whose worker dies before acknowledging it is re-queued and delivered to another worker.

item0.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns · Competing Consumers
item0.supports: The pattern's page in the public catalog: several consumers are created to receive from one point-to-point channel, the messaging system decides which of them receives each message, and the arrangement does not work on a publish-subscribe channel, where more consumers only make more copies. Its Kafka example notes that partitions settle in advance which consumer reads a message, so a consumer whose partition runs dry cannot help the others, and a consumer group cannot hold more competing consumers than the topic has partitions.

item1.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns (Hohpe and Woolf, Addison-Wesley, 2003) · Chapter 10: Messaging Endpoints, Competing Consumers
item1.supports: The book covers Competing Consumers in chapter 10, Messaging Endpoints; the publisher's page lists that chapter in its contents.

item2.title: DotLn · Execution guide (commit 9139d91)
item2.supports: Under independent workflows, the guide lets each work order's implementation and verification move on independently, with two orders routinely running side by side, each in its own worktree, and how much runs at once limited by the actors on hand and by a single writer per worktree. Under its discipline, a reservation tied to the session and its harness process turns away a second live writer, and when two sessions race to take over a dead holder's reservation only one becomes the writer.

item3.title: zip.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item3.supports: At the installed version zip keeps one buffer per source and pushes each value onto its own source's buffer; once every buffer holds a value it takes the oldest from each and emits them together, and it completes when a completed source's buffer is empty.

item4.title: RxJS guide · Testing RxJS code with marble diagrams (source at 7.8.2)
item4.supports: The marble syntax this example and its spec share: a dash is one frame, a letter an emission and a bar completion, and in subscription marbles a caret and an exclamation mark give the frames a subscription starts and ends, which is how each work stream is placed from the frame a session takes its order to the frame it finishes.

limits.item0: It needs a point-to-point channel and interchangeable consumers. On a topic the three sessions would each receive every order, as the companion study shows; and if some orders can be worked only by some sessions, a free session may be handed one it cannot work. Route such orders first, with a Content-Based Router, to a queue for each kind.
limits.item1: Taking turns is not the same as being free. When order 34 is handed out, Session 1, which took the first order and so would be next in a strict rotation through the three sessions, is still busy with the longest order, and the queue gives order 34 to Session 2 because Session 2 is free. RabbitMQ deals in turn by default, which would leave order 34 waiting behind order 31 while Session 2 sat idle; giving each consumer at most one unacknowledged message at a time, as its prefetch of one does, is what sends the next order to a session that is free.
limits.item2: Sequence is lost across consumers. Orders leave the queue in the order they were sent but are finished in whatever order their work allows: here order 33 is finished before order 31. When related messages must be handled in sequence, send them all to one consumer, as a broker partitioned by key does, or put the results back in order with a Resequencer.
limits.item3: A queue absorbs a burst, not a lasting excess. Order 34 waits until a session is free; if orders kept arriving faster than the sessions finish them, the queue would grow without end. Add consumers until they keep up, or slow the sender; RabbitMQ's tutorial warns that its queue fills up when every worker is busy.
limits.item4: Handing over is not finishing. Once an order is given to a session no other session can have it, so if that session fails partway the order is lost, unless the queue waits for an acknowledgement and hands an unacknowledged order to another session. Then the same order may be worked twice, so its work should be safe to repeat: see Transactional Client and Idempotent Receiver.
limits.item5: The analogy breaks at how exactly one is reached. In DotLn each order is worked in a checkout of its own, and a lock lets only one session write there, turning a second one away; nothing hands orders out to whichever session is free. A lock refuses the session that arrives second, where a queue never offers the order to it at all.

item0.why: A Publish-Subscribe Channel is the choice when every session needs every order, a copy each, rather than a share of them; the companion study runs these same orders over a topic.

item1.why: A Point-to-Point Channel is the channel this pattern stands on: read it for what a queue promises one receiver before several compete for it.

item2.why: A Message Dispatcher is the choice when one consumer should take every message off the channel and hand each to a performer it picks, so the application, not the broker, decides who works what.

item3.why: A Transactional Client is the choice when an order a session took but failed to finish must go back on the queue rather than be lost.

item4.why: An Idempotent Receiver is the choice when redelivery can hand the same order to a second session and working it twice must do no harm.

item5.why: A Resequencer is the choice when the results of orders worked at the same time must come out in the order the orders were sent.

item6.why: A Content-Based Router is the choice when the sessions are not interchangeable, so each kind of order must go to the queue of the sessions that can work it.

intuition.text: Picture a sorting desk with a short list of rules pinned above it. Each message is read once, the rules are tried from the top, and the first one that fits names the single channel the message leaves on. The sender never learns where its message went, the message is neither changed nor copied, and because sooner or later a message fits no rule, the list ends with a default.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public execution guide: a verifier reviewing a change files findings, and the guide sends each finding one of three ways according to what it shows. A finding that leaves one of the work's acceptance criteria unmet, or that a test probe shows breaking something the main branch already did, is blocking: the verification fails and the change goes back to the executor to be repaired. A decision that belongs to the operator, the person directing the work, goes to the operator, and any other defect becomes a follow-up, written up on the board of later work. One level up, the verification's result routes the change the same way: a failure sends it back for repair, a pass lets it go on to final review. The rule table is two tests and a default, written down in one place, and keeping it that small and that visible is what keeps a router maintainable.

example.name: Five findings from one verification
example.description: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public execution guide. The verifier files five findings, {findings}, one every other step from step 1 to step 9, and the findings end at step 10. The finding router tries its routes in the order {rules}. F1 leaves acceptance criterion 2 unmet; F2 is a stale line in an index; F3 asks to widen the scope of the work, a decision for the operator alone; F4 is a regression, something the main branch already did that test probe 3 shows broken; F5 leaves criterion 4 unmet and also asks whether to waive it. The router holds each finding for one step while it chooses, then sends it, unchanged, on the one channel its first passing rule names.

step0.title: Keep a short rule table, in order
step0.text: The router holds its rules as an ordered list: blocking when a finding has an unmet criterion or a regression, operator when it names a decision for the operator. The order is part of the rules, because one finding can pass more than one test.

step1.title: Try the rules from the top
step1.text: For each finding, test the rules in order and stop at the first that passes; that rule names the route. F5 passes both tests and is blocking, because the blocking rule is tried first.

step2.title: Fall back to the default
step2.text: A finding that passes no test, as F2 does, takes the default route, follow-up. Without a default it would have nowhere to go.

step3.title: Send it on one channel, unchanged
step3.text: The finding leaves on the channel its route names, exactly as it arrived: nothing is added, removed or copied, so each finding reaches one destination.

step4.title: End with the findings
step4.text: When the verifier's findings end, every channel ends too. The router keeps nothing between one finding and the next, so it has nothing left to send.

pseudocode.ordinary:
rules, tried in this order:
  blocking   if the finding has an unmet criterion or a regression
  operator   if the finding names a decision for the operator

on each finding from the verifier:
  route = the first rule in the list whose test the finding passes

  if no rule passed:
    route = follow-up

  send the finding, unchanged, on the channel that route names

when the verifier's findings end:
  end the blocking, operator and follow-up channels

item0.relevance: Apache Camel is an open-source Java integration framework whose routes are assembled from the integration patterns by name. Its Choice EIP is its content-based router, and this page documents it for the 4.22 long-term-support line.
item0.explanation: A choice holds an ordered list of when clauses, each a predicate, often a Simple-language test on a header, with the steps to run when it holds, and an optional otherwise. The first when that matches picks the branch and otherwise runs when none does; the page notes that otherwise is optional and that, without it, a message no predicate matches selects no branch. It adds a precondition mode that evaluates the predicates once at start-up, from property placeholders, system properties or environment variables, so every message takes the same branch: a router configured by deployment rather than by content.

item1.relevance: Spring Integration is the Spring portfolio's implementation of the integration patterns for Java applications. This page describes the routers it ships for content-based routing, and the page itself says most real cases delegate the decision to a plain Java object.
item1.explanation: A PayloadTypeRouter maps the payload's type to a channel and a HeaderValueRouter maps the value of one named header to a channel, configured in XML or in the Java DSL. A message whose header value has no mapping goes to the default output channel. By default a router must deliver each message to at least one channel, and dropping messages has to be asked for by pointing the default output channel at nullChannel. For its exception-type router, which matches the causes of an error against its mappings, the page notes that the order of the mappings matters.

item2.relevance: Kafka Streams is the stream-processing library of Apache Kafka. BranchedKStream, which KStream.split() returns, is how it sends each record of a stream to one of several branches; this is its API documentation for version 3.9.
item2.explanation: Branches are declared in order, each with a predicate, and each record goes to the first branch whose predicate is true and to that branch only. A record that matches none goes to the default branch, or is dropped when no default branch was declared, and the routing is stateless and record by record. To send one record to several streams, the page says to apply one filter per predicate to the same stream instead of branching.

item2.title: DotLn execution guide · Verification review and attack
item2.supports: DotLn's execution guide sorts every verification finding onto one of three routes: blocking, which fails the verification, for an unmet acceptance criterion or for a behaviour of main that the change breaks and a probe or fixture demonstrates; operator, for a written decision only the operator can take; and follow-up, reproduced and put on the board, for any other defect. The verifier may send a finding down the blocking route without asking anyone, and may not use the operator route to seek permission for a repair within the order's criteria.

limits.item0: Every destination is written into the router. A fourth route, such as a security review, means changing the rule table and everything that tests it. When destinations come and go, or each receiver knows best what it wants, a Publish-Subscribe Channel with a Message Filter on each receiver, or a Dynamic Router that receivers register with, moves that knowledge out of the router.
limits.item1: Overlapping rules make their order a decision. F5 passes both tests and is blocking only because that rule is tried first; with the two lines swapped it would go to the operator as a request to authorise a repair inside the criteria, the very route the guide rules out. A table grown large enough that nobody can see its overlaps is the point where a rules engine, or a split into smaller routers, earns its cost.
limits.item2: A default route hides format drift. If the verifier began filing an unmet criterion under a renamed field, F1 would pass no test and reach the board as a follow-up: a blocking finding quietly made harmless, with nothing failing. Where no default is safe, send what matches nothing to an Invalid Message Channel and watch it. The guide's final review guards the same seam: a finding with a route outside the three, or a failed review that lists no blocking finding, leaves the review's counts unmeasured and draws an advisory naming the cause.
limits.item3: The router sees one message at a time and keeps nothing. A rule that needs history is not content-based: DotLn's drive, the loop that takes an order through its phases, stops after three failed verifications, which takes a count kept across reports, and that belongs in a stateful component such as a Process Manager, not in the router.
limits.item4: The analogy breaks where the platform routes by judgement. The verifier decides each route while it writes its immutable report, from evidence it has reproduced; nothing reads a field and nothing travels on a channel per route. The pattern needs the destination to be computable from the message alone, which is why each finding in this example carries the field its route depends on.

item0.why: Reach for a Message Filter when there is one destination and the only question is whether a message goes there at all.

item1.why: Reach for a Recipient List when one message must go to several destinations at once, not to exactly one.

item2.why: Reach for a Dynamic Router when the destinations change at run time and each announces which messages it wants, so the rule table is built from their registrations.

item3.why: Reach for an Invalid Message Channel as the destination of messages no rule should accept, instead of a default route that treats them as ordinary.

item4.why: Reach for a Publish-Subscribe Channel with a filter on each receiver when receivers should decide for themselves and no central rule table is wanted.

item5.why: Read the router trade-offs when weighing a central rule table that every change touches against routing spread across receivers, where the dependencies are harder to see.

item6.why: Reach for a Routing Slip when a message must visit several steps in an order decided at the start, rather than one destination.

flow.caption: Each token is one finding, numbered as the verifier numbers it: token 1 is F1, and so on to 5. The Verifier reviews a change and files the findings. The Finding router reads each one, holds it for a step while it chooses, then sends it on. The Executor, which repairs the change, receives blocking findings; the Operator, the person directing the work, receives decisions that are theirs alone; the Board, a list of later work, receives everything else as a follow-up. The words in a box say what that box holds or has decided, and a destination's words start with the route it receives. A token is green while it moves and outlined while a box holds it, and a box a token leaves or reaches is outlined in green.

intuition.text: Management gets a road of its own. Each component keeps two doors: at one, work arrives and waits its turn; at the other, questions and commands arrive and are dealt with before the next piece of work. Because the two never share a queue, a pause is not stuck behind a backlog, a status question does not disturb the work it asks about, and no work record has to be opened to find out whether it is secretly a command.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public execution guide (its Operator recovery controls section): an order's records pass from role to role as work, while the operator's exact phrases are messages of another kind. analysis: halts what a session is doing so that the operator can diagnose it, holds on to its unfinished work and waits to be told how to go on; operator override: stops DotLn's hooks, the automatic guards that can refuse an action, from vetoing the operator's instructions until operator override: off; and neither phrase starts a phase of the work or records a pass. Keeping those phrases on a channel of their own, never mixed into the work records, is the discipline this pattern names. The same guide calls the main checkout the control plane and gives the harness commands about that machinery itself: writer --show tells a refused session which other session holds the right to write in a worktree, and evidence --stop halts a session's own gate, its run of checks, without recording a pass. In the same analogy those are control messages about the control plane.

example.name: The operator pauses the verifier while evidence keeps coming
example.description: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public execution guide: the executor puts the evidence of orders 31, 32 and 33 on the work queue, and the verifier takes it one record at a time. On the control bus the operator first asks both roles for their status, then sends {pause} to the verifier while 32 waits in the work queue, and later gives the direction {direction}. The bus carries only questions, commands and answers; the work queue carries only evidence.

step0.title: Give every component two ports
step0.text: Each role takes work from its work queue in turn and listens separately on its control port, which it reads before it takes the next work record. The control bus joins the operator to every control port and to nothing else.

step1.title: Ask on the bus
step1.text: A status question goes out on the bus to every role's control port. Each role answers about itself, on the bus, and the answers come back to the operator. No work record moves to produce them, so the picture they give is of the flow as it stands.

step2.title: Command on the bus
step2.text: A command such as {pause} is addressed to one role. The role acts on it before it takes another work record, however much work is waiting in its queue, and keeps the record it holds.

step3.title: Work goes on regardless
step3.text: A command on the bus reaches only the role it is addressed to. The senders on the work queue were sent no pause, so work keeps arriving for the paused role and waits in its queue, and the backlog grows for as long as the pause lasts.

step4.title: Resume on direction
step4.text: The direction {direction} returns the role to its interrupted routine, starting with the record it kept, so the pause has lost nothing and reordered nothing.

pseudocode.ordinary:
for each role:
  workQueue = its place on the work queue
  controlPort = its place on the control bus
  loop:
    handle every message waiting at controlPort
    if not paused: take the next record from workQueue

operator sends "status?" on the control bus to every role
each role answers on the control bus: what it works on, what it holds
the operator reads the answers; no work record moves for them

operator sends pause to the verifier on the control bus
the verifier, before its next work record:
  stops its routine and keeps the record it holds

the executor, which was sent no pause, puts the next evidence on the work queue
it waits there with the rest, untouched

operator sends direction to the verifier on the control bus
the verifier resumes its routine with the record it kept

item0.project: Apache Camel, the Control Bus component
item0.relevance: Apache Camel is an open-source integration framework from the Apache Software Foundation. Its Control Bus component is the framework's own reading of this pattern: the page presents it as a way to watch and steer a running Camel application by sending it messages.
item0.explanation: A route or a test sends an ordinary message to a controlbus: endpoint, and the endpoint acts on the running application instead of passing the message on. The route command takes a routeId and an action, one of start, stop, suspend, resume, restart, fail, status and stats, and can return a route's status, or its performance statistics as XML, in the reply. The language command evaluates the message body as an expression, such as a Simple expression that calls the route controller. The page also lists the other ways in that Camel keeps, JMX, a Java API on the CamelContext and the event notifier, so the bus is one door among several; its async option runs a task without putting the result on the exchange.

item1.relevance: Spring Integration is the Spring portfolio's messaging and integration framework. Its reference has a Control Bus page in its System Management part.
item1.explanation: A control-bus endpoint listens on an input channel for messages whose payload names an operation as beanName.methodName, with any arguments in a dedicated header, and invokes that operation on a bean in the application context; a return value can be sent on to an output channel. Only operations an application has chosen to expose qualify: methods annotated @ManagedAttribute or @ManagedOperation, Spring's Lifecycle and Pausable methods and some executor and scheduler settings, so the same methods serve JMX and the bus. Because the bus can change the system's state, the page recommends securing what it receives, and it points to a REST controller for reaching the bus over HTTP.

item2.project: Spring Cloud Bus, its bus endpoints
item2.relevance: Spring Cloud Bus gives a Spring Boot application bus versions of three actuator endpoints, so that one request can act on the instances joined to the bus instead of on one. It is a control bus built for a single job: carrying a management instruction to every running copy of an application.
item2.explanation: Three endpoints, /actuator/busrefresh, /actuator/busenv and /actuator/busshutdown, correspond to the single-instance refresh, env and shutdown endpoints. busrefresh clears the refresh-scope cache and rebinds configuration properties, busenv sets one key to one value in the environment of the instances on the bus, and busshutdown shuts an application down gracefully. Adding a bus id to the path addresses one instance instead of all of them. Each endpoint must be exposed in the application's configuration before it can be called.

item0.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns · Control Bus
item0.supports: The pattern's page sets the problem of managing a messaging system whose parts sit on many platforms in many places, and answers it with management traffic that uses the same messaging as the application but channels of its own, so that every component is joined both to the application's flow and to the control bus.

item1.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns (Hohpe and Woolf, Addison-Wesley, 2003), chapter 11, System Management, section Control Bus
item1.supports: The book covers the Control Bus pattern in chapter 11, System Management; the publisher's page lists the book and that chapter in its table of contents.

item2.title: DotLn execution guide · Operator recovery controls
item2.supports: The platform's guide says that analysis: stops the current routine so that the operator can diagnose it, keeps unfinished work and waits for direction; that operator override: stops the hooks from vetoing the operator for the rest of that session, until operator override: off, and takes hold before any runtime code is loaded or repository state is checked; that neither phrase dispatches a phase or records a pass; and that diagnosis must still work when the worktree, lifecycle, runtime or gate is broken.

item3.title: DotLn execution guide · Discipline
item3.supports: The guide names the main checkout as the control plane; a session refused because another session holds the worktree's writer reservation runs node scripts/harness.mjs writer --show to learn who holds it; and node scripts/harness.mjs evidence --stop halts the session's own gate without recording a pass.

item4.title: DotLn execution guide · Operator resume phrases
item4.supports: The platform's status report is built from the order records in the current checkout, not from unmerged work in other worktrees, and asking for it, in either of its two forms, changes nothing and adds no record.

limits.item0: A status answer is a component's own account of itself. It shows that the control port responds, not that the work is right: a verifier could report the record it is checking while filing wrong reports, and the bus and the work queue can disagree, the bus calling a role healthy while its queue is stuck. To learn whether the work path still works, send a test message through it. DotLn's own resume: status works another way. It reads what each order's record in the checkout says and writes nothing, so it reports what was recorded rather than asking a live session what it is doing.
limits.item1: A pause stops one component, not its senders. The pause is addressed to the verifier alone, so the executor keeps putting evidence on the work queue, and the records pile up there until someone sends the direction to go on. An operator who forgets a paused component has stopped the flow as surely as a crash would; a pause needs an expiry or an alarm, or the senders need telling too.
limits.item2: The bus is a way in for anyone who can post to it, and a stop or a configuration change sent there acts on the running system. Spring Integration's page recommends securing the control bus's input for that reason. A control message needs a known sender and a bounded scope; DotLn's guide, for one, keeps operator override: to the session it was typed in, and the next session starts without it.
limits.item3: The pattern rides the same messaging infrastructure as the work, so when the broker or the network fails the bus fails with it, just when the operator needs it most. Here the analogy breaks: DotLn's guide asks the opposite of its recovery phrases. Diagnosis must still work when the worktree, the lifecycle, the runtime or a gate is broken, and the override takes hold before any runtime code is loaded or the repository's state is checked. A last-resort way in should not share the machinery it is meant to repair.
limits.item4: For a few components in one process, a second set of channels can cost more than it saves: every component keeps twice the connections, and both sets need configuring and securing. Direct management calls, or management messages carried in band with the risk that a command waits behind work, can be enough there.

item0.why: Read this trade-off when deciding whether separate control channels earn their cost, or whether in-band management will do.

item1.why: Read the kinds of control message, configuration, heartbeat, test, exception and statistics, when deciding what a bus should carry beyond a pause and a status question.

item2.why: Reach for a test message when you need to know that a component still processes correctly; an answer on the bus shows only that it is alive.

item3.why: Use a detour when the operator should switch messages through extra validation or debugging steps from the bus, rather than pause or question a component.

item4.why: Use a message store when the question is what has passed through the flow, answered later from copies, rather than what a component is doing now.

item5.why: A dynamic router is fed by a control channel too: read it when control messages should reconfigure where work goes rather than stop a component.

example.caption: Each token is one message. 31, 32 and 33 are the evidence of those orders, which the Executor puts on the Work queue for the Verifier. On the Control bus, s is the Operator's status question, e and v are the Executor's and the Verifier's answers, p is the pause, analysis:, and g is the go-ahead. The Executor and the Verifier are the two roles doing the work, and the Operator is the person steering them. The Work queue and the Control bus are the two channels every role is joined to: the queue carries only evidence and holds what the Verifier has not yet taken, the bus carries only questions, commands and answers and holds nothing. The words in a box say what that box is doing, and the tokens in a box are the messages it holds. A token is green while it moves and outlined while a box holds it, and a box a token leaves or reaches is outlined in green.
