intuition.text: A correlation identifier is how a requestor tells replies apart. Requests leave in one order, the work finishes in another, and the replies share one channel, so a reply's position says nothing about which request caused it. The only reliable link is a value the reply carries back. With it a requestor can keep many requests open at once, give each reply to the one piece of work waiting for it, and recognise a reply that belongs to nobody.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public domain model. DotLn is the operator's platform for running AI agents on pieces of work, and its kernel is the part that decides what happens next and sends commands out. Each command carries an id of its own, a commandId; an adapter hands the command to a worker; and the result that comes back (a CommandResult) is matched to its command by the commandId it carries. Even the acknowledgement that a command was accepted (a CommandReceipt) names the commandId it answers. Here the kernel sends out three commands at once, and their results come back in the order the workers finish. The need grows wherever work fans out: the domain model's OpinionCohort, a set of opinions gathered on one question, groups its results under one cohort id while each opinion keeps its own command, so gathering them depends on every answer naming what it answers.

example.name: Three commands out at once
example.description: As an analogy, read against DotLn's domain model. The Kernel sends {commands} to three workers, one per step, each command carrying its id, and opens one wait, an Await, for each. The workers answer on one shared Results channel in the order they finish, {replyOrder}, and each result carries the id of the command it answers. A result sits on the channel for one step, and then the Await whose id it names takes it; the other Awaits leave it alone. At the end Worker 2 sends a second copy of its result, and the copy finds no Await open.

step0.title: Stamp each request with its own id
step0.text: The requestor gives every request an id that no other pending request shares, and remembers it until the reply comes. Here the kernel sends {commands}, each with its commandId, and opens an Await for each.

step1.title: Copy the id into the reply
step1.text: The replier does not make up an id: it copies the one from the request into its reply. Each worker's result names the commandId it answers, so the result can be placed without knowing who sent it or when.

step2.title: Match on the id, never on the order
step2.text: Results share one channel and arrive in the order the work finishes, {replyOrder} here. Each pending request takes only the result carrying its own id and leaves the rest. In the RxJS reading each pending command is one subscription to result$, which first() ends at the result naming it; the delay(1) after it only lets taking the result show as a step of its own.

step3.title: Forget the id once it is answered
step3.text: A request that has its reply stops waiting. A second copy of that reply, or a reply for a request nobody waits for, then matches nothing and is dropped, as the repeated result for cmd_2 is.

pseudocode.ordinary:
to send a request:
  id = a new id that no pending request uses
  pending[id] = the work waiting for this reply
  send the request with id

replier, on each request:
  do the work
  send the reply with correlation id = the request's id

on each reply, in whatever order replies arrive:
  waiter = pending[the reply's correlation id]
  if there is a waiter:
    give the reply to that waiter only

once a waiter has its reply:
  delete pending[its id]
  a later reply with that id finds no waiter: drop it

item0.relevance: Apache Camel is an open-source integration framework built around these patterns. Its Correlation Identifier page shows where the id lives in a framework that mostly sets it for you.
item0.explanation: A correlation id is a header on the message. Over JMS the JMSCorrelationID header is set and matched automatically, so a route rarely needs its own; a route can still add one to tie a whole conversation together, which the page connects to distributed tracing. The patterns that spin off new messages, Enrich, Multicast, Recipient List, Split and Wire Tap, put the source exchange's id on each new exchange as a CORRELATION_ID property, so every part can be traced back to the exchange it came from.

item1.relevance: Spring Integration is the Spring portfolio's messaging framework. Its JMS outbound gateway sends a request to a JMS destination and waits for the reply, and its reference lists how each configuration makes sure a gateway receives only replies to its own requests.
item1.explanation: With no correlation key, the gateway expects the replier to copy the request's JMSMessageID into the reply's JMSCorrelationID and selects the reply on that; with a key, the gateway generates a unique id, puts it in the named property and selects on it. With a shared reply listener the id is the gateway's own id plus an incrementing number, so several gateways can share one reply destination and each picks out its own replies. The page warns that the gateway cannot ensure a supplied correlation id is unique and that a repeated one can have unexpected side effects.

item2.relevance: RabbitMQ is an open-source message broker. Its sixth tutorial builds a remote procedure call over queues and explains why that call needs a correlation id.
item2.explanation: The client receives every reply on one reply pseudo-queue, so it sets a unique correlation_id on each request and the server copies it into its response. The client hands a response back only when the id matches, and quietly discards one with an unknown id rather than failing: a server that dies after answering but before acknowledging the request will process it again after a restart, so duplicate responses are expected and the call should ideally be idempotent.

item2.title: DotLn · product document 02, Domain model, at commit 9139d91
item2.supports: The platform's kernel vocabulary: a Command carries a stable, kernel-computed commandId; a CommandResult is matched on payload.commandId, and a CommandReceipt carries the commandId it acknowledges; the commandId hash is namespace-tagged because without the tag two distinct commands could collide and the outbox's idempotence guard would silently swallow one; replay keeps a result that comes before its command was recorded and completes the command once that record arrives; Await waits for an event matching a commandId or correlationId and carries a timeout; and an OpinionCohort is a set of result envelopes correlated by a cohort id, each opinion keeping its own command.

item3.title: DotLn · product document 03, Architecture, at commit 9139d91
item3.supports: The platform's outbox protocol correlates a result by commandId; its failure matrix ignores a duplicate result deterministically by commandId, leaves state unchanged and records the dedup in the trace; and after a lease expires a fresh attempt gets a new episode id but keeps the stable command id.

limits.item0: Matching by arrival order instead of by id works only while one request is out at a time or the replier answers strictly in turn. With three commands out here, pairing results with commands in the order they were sent would give cmd_1 the failure of cmd_3, cmd_2 the completion of cmd_1 and cmd_3 the blocked status of cmd_2, and nothing would look wrong.
limits.item1: The id matches a reply; it does not make one arrive. In this pipeline first() has no deadline, so a command whose result is lost holds its wait open for ever. Give each wait a deadline, as the kernel's Await carries a timeout beside its pattern, and decide what a reply arriving after it means: by then it matches nothing, just like the repeated result for cmd_2.
limits.item2: Dropping a reply nobody waits for is silent. That is right for a harmless repeat, such as a retried worker's result with the same commandId, but it hides a fault when the copy disagrees with the first answer or when replies are going astray. Count unmatched replies rather than discarding them unseen, or put an idempotent receiver in front that records what it has already accepted. DotLn's architecture ignores a repeated result by its commandId and notes in its trace that it did, where this pipeline drops the copy only because nobody is listening any more.
limits.item3: An id has to be unique among pending requests and must not be reused while an old reply could still arrive. DotLn's domain model records why its commandId hash is namespace-tagged: without the tag, two different commands could share an id, and the check that stops a command running twice would silently drop one of them. Spring Integration's JMS gateway likewise warns that it cannot ensure a supplied correlation id is unique.
limits.item4: A wait has to exist before its reply arrives. result$ here is hot and keeps nothing, so a result that came before its command's Await opened would be missed and the Await would wait for ever. DotLn's replay handles that order explicitly: it keeps a result that arrives before its command has been recorded, and completes the command once the record arrives.

item0.why: The exchange the identifier serves: one request and one reply on two channels. While a single request is out at a time, the reply channel alone tells the requestor what a reply is for, and no id is needed yet.

item1.why: When choosing what the id should be, a generated id as commandId is here or a business key such as the order the work is for, and how to follow a chain of requests in which each answer starts the next request.

item2.why: The id says which request a reply answers; a return address says where the reply should go. A replier that serves several requestors usually needs both.

item3.why: When each requestor should receive only its own replies from a shared channel, so the filtering on the id happens at the channel rather than in every waiting request.

item4.why: When several replies belong together and should become one result, grouped by a shared id, as DotLn's OpinionCohort groups its opinions under a cohort id.

item5.why: When a repeated reply has to be recognised and recorded, not just dropped because nothing waits for it any more.

It delivers whether or not anything listens, so D is drawn on it although nothing takes it. resumed$ is each result handed to the wait it matched, one frame after it arrived.

The Kernel is the part of DotLn that sends the commands. Worker 1, 2 and 3 each run one command. Results is the one channel every worker answers on, so results arrive in the order the work finishes. Await 1, 2 and 3 are the Kernel's waits, one for each command sent, and each takes only the result naming its command's id. The words in a box say what that box is doing. intuition.text: An event message reports a change and stops there. The sender does not know who is listening or what they will do with the news; each receiver decides for itself, and another can start listening without the sender changing at all. What the message mostly carries is a moment, often no more than which change and when, so a receiver's first question is how old it is: an announcement that was true when it was sent says less about the present with every minute that passes.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public domain model: an Event there is an unchangeable record that something happened, stamped with the time it occurred; the event store keeps every one and leaves its meaning to whoever reacts, and watchers, read-only views of that store, each tell their own story from the same events. Each work order also has a control beacon, a small record of the order's phase and latest verdict, stamped with the time of its last transition; an agent's sweep reads it and labels it fresh, or stale once its age reaches a threshold of twenty minutes by default. So the entries recording each step of an order, and the beacons, both read as time-stamped announcements that others react to. Here order 41 passes verification and later moves to final review, and the second beacon write fails, as DotLn's execution guide allows a beacon write to do while the change itself stays recorded.

example.name: Order 41's beacon through verification and final review
example.description: As an analogy to DotLn's records of a work order: at 10:00 order {order} passes verification, and the lifecycle, the part of DotLn that records each step of an order, sends the news to the event store and then writes it to the order's beacon. Both watchers read the entry and each draws its own conclusion, and the sweep at 10:05 finds the beacon fresh. At 10:12 the order moves to final review: the news reaches the event store, but the beacon write fails. The sweep at 10:30 reads the old announcement, now past the {staleAfter}-minute threshold, and labels it stale.

step0.title: Announce it as it happens
step0.text: When the change happens, the sender records what changed and when and sends it straight away, here to the event store and to the order's beacon. It names no receiver and asks for nothing.

step1.title: Each receiver decides what it means
step1.text: Every reader of the event store gets the same entry and draws its own conclusion. The sender neither knows nor cares who they are, and a new reader changes nothing at the sender.

step2.title: Judge the age before believing it
step2.text: A reader compares the event's time with its own clock. Younger than {staleAfter} minutes, the announcement is fresh; at or past that it is stale, kept as history but not taken as the present.

step3.title: A missing announcement leaves the last one standing
step3.text: If a later change never reaches a channel, that channel's readers go on seeing the earlier event. Nothing in the old message is false; only its age shows that it may be out of date.

pseudocode.ordinary:
when order 41 passes verification:
  event = { change: verified, verdict: pass, at: now }
  append event to the event store
  write event to the order's beacon

for each watcher of the event store:
  on each new entry: update its own account of the order
  (the entry carries no instruction)

when a sweep reads the beacon:
  age = time of the sweep - beacon.at
  if age >= staleAfter: label it stale, keep it as history
  otherwise: label it fresh

when order 41 moves to final review:
  append the new event to the event store
  write it to the beacon
  (if that write fails, the beacon goes on showing the old event)

visual.textEquivalent: Order {order}, step {step}: {moves}. On the event store and the beacon, and at the watchers and the sweep, whose threshold is {staleAfter} minutes: {states}. Held: {held}.

item0.explanation: Camel treats an event message as a matter of direction rather than content: an exchange marked InOnly tells the producing endpoint that no reply is expected. Components that can work both ways, such as JMS, SEDA and AMQP, then send and move on, and many, JMS, File and SEDA among them, are one-way by default. item1.explanation: An ApplicationEventListeningMessageProducer listens to the application context and sends each event it hears to a channel, optionally only the event types it is configured for; the page's example uses a publish-subscribe channel, so every subscriber gets each one. item2.title: DotLn product documents · 02 Domain model, at commit 9139d91
item2.supports: DotLn's domain model defines an Event as an immutable observation that occurred, with occurredAt in its envelope; keeps events in an append-only event store that leaves payload meaning to reactors; describes watchers that each tell their own story from one set of events; defines a control beacon whose size is a code for the order's phase and latest verdict and whose modification time is the appended transition's recordedAt; and labels a swept beacon stale once its age reaches staleAfterMs, twenty minutes by default, or clock-skew when its time is after the sweep, and notes that a beacon's age never alters what an actor may do or which transitions are legal.

item3.title: DotLn product documents · 07 Execution guide, at commit 9139d91
item3.supports: DotLn's execution guide has every recorded state change rewrite the order's beacon, keeps the change recorded even when that rewrite only warns, and sweeps with a twenty-minute age limit unless told otherwise.

limits.item0: A missed announcement leaves the last one standing. From 10:12 the event store has the move to final review while the beacon still says verified at 10:00, and only its age gives it away. Had the threshold been an hour instead of {staleAfter} minutes, the 10:30 sweep would have reported as fresh a phase the order had already left. Expiry protects only as well as its threshold matches how often the source should speak; a reader that must be right reads the full record, here the event store.
limits.item1: Nobody is obliged to act. An event names no receiver, so if the one party that had to respond is not listening, the change is announced, nothing happens and nothing reports an error. When exactly one party must do something, send it a Command Message, and the event as well if others should know.
limits.item2: A receiver that is not listening misses the event. On a plain publish-subscribe channel, a watcher that starts late or is down never sees what was sent meanwhile. DotLn's event store keeps every entry for replay, so the analogy hides this failure; where receivers come and go, reach for a Durable Subscriber or a store that can be replayed.
limits.item3: A thin event sends its receivers back for the facts. An event that says only that something changed makes every interested receiver fetch the details, multiplying the load on the source and racing any change made in between; when receivers need the content, a Document Message, or an event that carries the new state, serves better.
limits.item4: Times from different clocks can disagree. An event stamped by a clock that runs ahead looks younger than it is, and one stamped in the reader's future would pass any age check; DotLn's domain model labels such a beacon clock-skew rather than fresh. Compare ages only where the clocks are trusted, or order events by a sequence from a single source.
limits.item5: The analogy bends: DotLn's beacon is read when a sweep looks rather than delivered to anyone, and it keeps only the order's latest state, so it behaves like a polled channel holding one message, not a stream of events. A reader that sweeps rarely sees the newest phase and none of those in between.

item0.why: Reach for a command message when one receiver must carry out a particular action, rather than whoever listens choosing how to react.

item1.why: Reach for a document message when the content matters more than the moment, such as a verification report that its receivers read in full.

item2.why: The publish-subscribe channel is what hands each listener its own copy of an announcement; read it for how that fan-out behaves on its own.

item3.why: A durable subscriber is the answer when a receiver that was offline must still get every event sent while it was away.

item4.why: Message expiration lets the sender stamp when an event stops being worth delivering, instead of leaving every reader to judge its age.

item5.why: A polling consumer checks a channel when it chooses, as the beacon's sweeps do, instead of being called when a message arrives.

start.note: Nothing has moved yet: order 41 is still being verified.

0.note: At 10:00 the verification passes, and the lifecycle sends v, the news of it, to the event store as it happens. v names no reader and asks nothing of anyone.

1.note: Because of that entry, the lifecycle also writes v to the order’s beacon, replacing what the beacon said before.

2.note: The event store hands v to both watchers. Each draws its own conclusion; neither was told what to do, and the lifecycle knows of neither.

3.note: At 10:05 the sweep reads v from the beacon. The news is under the threshold, so the sweep labels it fresh; reading it leaves it on the beacon.

4.note: At 10:12 the order moves to final review, and the lifecycle sends r, the news of it, to the event store.

5.note: The lifecycle tries to write r to the beacon, but the write fails with a warning. Nothing reaches the beacon, so it still holds v.

6.note: The event store hands r to both watchers, so anyone reading the event store sees the order in final review.

7.note: At 10:30 the sweep reads the beacon again and gets v. It still says verified, but it is past the {{threshold}}-minute threshold, so the sweep labels it stale instead of reporting a phase the order has left.

example.caption: Each box is one part of the example. The Lifecycle, the part of DotLn that records each step of a work order, announces every change to order 41. The Event store pipe keeps every announcement for whoever reads it, and the Quality watcher and Intent watcher each read it and keep their own account. The event messages, v and r, are what the pattern is about; Beacon, the pipe with the bold name, is the channel where their age is judged: it keeps only the latest announcement, and the Sweep, an agent that looks at it now and then, judges how old that is. A token is a message: v is the news that order 41 was verified at 10:00, and r is the news that it moved to final review at 10:12; the same letter in two boxes is the same news on two channels. A token is green while it moves and outlined inside the box that holds it; a box a message leaves or reaches is outlined in green, and the words inside each box say what it knows or is doing. Reading the beacon leaves its token in place. Step forward to move the messages on.

intuition.text: Guaranteed delivery makes ‘sent’ a promise about disks rather than about memory. Every hand-over has two halves: the next holder writes the message down and says so, and only then does the previous holder let go. The price is that a crash between a hand-over and its acknowledgement repeats the hand-over, so a message may arrive twice, but no crash the stores survive can make it vanish.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's architecture document. It describes a host program that writes each event to its log on disk, and syncs the disk, before its decision logic moves on; a command reaches the program that carries it out only once the command is in that log; and a worker's finished result is saved as a receipt, never changed afterwards, before the result is recorded. A crash between those writes leaves a command still open, for a later recovery to finish, rather than a lost one. The rule worth carrying into any hand-off between agents follows: write to the log before acknowledging, and treat a receipt as the acknowledgement, never as the only copy.

example.name: A command that survives a crash
example.description: As an analogy, read against DotLn's architecture document: a host sends command 7 to a worker on another machine. Each side keeps a store on disk, the host's outbox and the worker's inbox. The outbox forwards the command and lets go of it only when the inbox says it has saved it; the inbox hands it to the worker and keeps it until the worker's receipt. The worker's machine crashes at step {crashStep}, after the command arrived and before the receipt, so after the restart the inbox delivers it again. The document names an outbox, receipts and recovery but no store on the worker's side: the inbox is the pattern's, not the platform's.

step0.title: Save before the send returns
step0.text: The host writes the command to its outbox and syncs the disk before sending returns to it. From this moment a copy is always on some disk.

step1.title: Let go only when the next store has saved it
step1.text: The outbox forwards a copy to the inbox and keeps its own until the inbox confirms that it has written the command down. Between the forward and the confirmation, two disks hold it.

step2.title: Delete only on the receiver's receipt
step2.text: The inbox hands the command to the worker and keeps its copy until the worker acknowledges. When the worker's machine crashes at step {crashStep}, the worker loses what it held in memory and the inbox's copy is untouched.

step3.title: Send again what is still held after a restart
step3.text: On restart each store sends again whatever it still holds. The worker can therefore receive the same command twice, and must recognise it by its id wherever doing the work twice would be wrong.

pseudocode.ordinary:
send(command):
  write command to the outbox
  sync the outbox's disk
  return (only now is the send done)

for each command in the outbox:
  copy it to the inbox
  wait until the inbox says it is saved
  delete the outbox's copy

for each command in the inbox:
  hand it to the worker
  wait for the worker's receipt
  delete the inbox's copy

after any restart:
  each store sends again what it still holds
  the worker skips a command id it has already finished

visual.textEquivalent: Step {step}: {moves}; {held}; {states}. From the send to the receipt a copy of the command stays on the Outbox's or the Inbox's disk; the worker's copy is only in memory.

item0.relevance: Apache Camel is a Java integration framework whose routes are assembled from the book's patterns; its documentation has a page for this one.
item0.explanation: The page names the components through which Camel provides the guarantee: File, which keeps messages in the file system, JMS and Kafka with persistent delivery, JPA, and database components such as SQL, JDBC and MyBatis. item1.relevance: Spring Integration is Spring's implementation of the book's patterns inside an application. It has no page named for Guaranteed Delivery; this section, on persistent queue channels, is where the guarantee is configured, for a channel inside one application.
item1.explanation: A QueueChannel keeps its messages in memory by default, so a failure can lose them. Given a persistent message store, such as JdbcChannelMessageStore, the channel writes each message to the store when it arrives and takes it out when a consumer polls it. With a transactional store and a poller running in a transaction, taking a message out is undone if that transaction fails, so the message is still in the store to be tried again.

item2.relevance: RabbitMQ is a message broker; its guide to consumer acknowledgements and publisher confirms (version 4.4 when read) documents both halves of the hand-over this pattern needs.
item2.explanation: With publisher confirms, the broker confirms a message marked persistent, sent to a queue that survives restarts, only once the message is on disk. It writes to disk in batches, to keep fsync calls few, so under steady load a confirm can take a few hundred milliseconds. The guide shows how, without confirms, a message the client assumed safe is lost when a node fails before writing it to disk. On the consumer side, under manual acknowledgement, a delivery not yet acknowledged goes back into the queue when its channel or connection closes, marked as a redelivery, so consumers must be ready to see a message twice.

item0.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns · Guaranteed Delivery
item0.supports: Each hop keeps its own durable copy of a message until the next hop has stored it and, at the end, the receiver has acknowledged it; a send is complete once the sender's own store has the message.

item1.title: Hohpe and Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns (Addison-Wesley, 2003), Chapter 4: Messaging Channels, Guaranteed Delivery

item2.title: DotLn architecture (docs/product/03-architecture.md) at commit 9139d91
item2.supports: DotLn's outbox protocol writes a command to the log before the program that carries it out receives it, matches the result to the command by its id, ignores a duplicate the same way every time, and keeps a command open, to be recovered, while its result has not arrived. Its inspection host writes and syncs each event to disk before moving on and saves each finished result as a receipt filed under its command and never changed; if it crashes between saving a receipt and recording the result, the command stays open and a later recovery reads the receipt. The document disclaims exactly-once effects on outside systems.

limits.item0: This is at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once. The crash at step {crashStep} falls between delivery and receipt, so the worker receives command 7 twice; had the worker finished the work and crashed before its receipt left, the work would run twice. Make the receiver recognise a repeat, or make receiving, working and acknowledging one transaction. DotLn's architecture document says the same of its own outbox: results are matched to commands by id and duplicates ignored, and nothing promises that an effect on an outside system happens only once.
limits.item1: Every hand-over waits for a disk write, so latency and throughput pay for the guarantee; RabbitMQ, for one, syncs persistent messages in batches and documents confirms taking a few hundred milliseconds under load. For messages whose loss costs little, such as frequent readings that the next one replaces, skip it.
limits.item2: A receiver that stays down lets its store, and then the stores behind it, grow until a disk fills, and the guarantee turns into failed sends. Give messages that can outlive their use a time limit, and watch the stores' depth.
limits.item3: The guarantee ends where the acknowledgement is given. A worker that sends its receipt on arrival, before doing the work, hands the risk back to memory: a crash after that receipt loses the work with no copy left to send again. Acknowledge after the work's effects are saved.
limits.item4: An in-memory buffer only looks similar. A ReplaySubject or a retry keeps or resends values while the process lives and loses them all when it dies; nothing in a stream library survives the crash this pattern is about, which is why this study is drawn step by step rather than run.
limits.item5: The analogy breaks at both ends. DotLn keeps its receipts immutable and treats a command as pending until its result is recorded, end to end, rather than deleting each copy hop by hop, and its document describes no store on the worker's side that holds a command before the worker takes it, as the inbox does here.

item0.why: Idempotent Receiver is the choice when the duplicates this pattern allows would do harm: the receiver recognises a message it has already handled and does nothing the second time.

item1.why: Transactional Client is the choice when receiving, working and acknowledging must succeed or fail together, so a crash cannot split the receipt from the work.

item2.why: Durable Subscriber is the publish-subscribe counterpart: when the receiver is a subscriber that may be offline, the channel keeps its messages until it returns.

item3.why: Message Expiration is the choice when a kept message can become worse than none: a limit lets a store set it aside instead of delivering it late.

item4.why: The costs of guaranteed delivery, and when to skip it, are the question to settle before paying for a disk write on every hand-over.

start.note: The host has decided to send command 7 to the worker. The command exists only in the host’s memory, and nothing is on any disk yet.

0.note: The host writes command 7 to its outbox and syncs the disk, and only then does its send return. From here on a copy is always on some disk.

1.note: The outbox forwards a copy to the worker’s inbox, which writes it to its own disk. The outbox keeps its copy: it has no word yet that the inbox saved it.

2.note: The inbox confirms that command 7 is on its disk, and only then does the outbox delete its copy. The inbox now holds the only copy.

3.note: The inbox hands command 7 to the worker, which starts on it. The inbox keeps its copy until the worker sends a receipt.

states.inbox: machine down; c safe on disk

4.note: The worker’s machine crashes before the worker has sent a receipt. The command the worker held in memory is gone; the inbox’s copy is on disk and untouched.

5.note: The machine restarts. The inbox reads its disk and finds command 7 still there, never acknowledged.

states.inbox: sent c again; still keeps it

6.note: The inbox delivers command 7 again. Whatever the worker did before the crash, it now sees the same command a second time, and its id is how it can tell.

7.note: The worker finishes and sends a receipt. Only now does the inbox delete its copy: command 7 has been delivered, and no disk needs to keep it.

example.caption: Each token is one message: c is command 7 itself, s is the Inbox’s word to the Outbox that it has saved c, and r is the Worker’s receipt for c. The Host decides to send the command, and the Outbox is the store on the Host’s disk. The Inbox is the store on the Worker’s machine, and the Worker carries the command out. The two stores are drawn as pipes because they are channels on disk, so a token they hold survives a crash; a token the Worker holds is only in its memory. The words in a box say what that box is doing or holding. A token is green while it moves and outlined while a box holds it, and a box a token leaves or reaches is outlined in green.

intuition.text: A channel gives each message to whoever takes it next; it has no idea who ought to do the work. Put a single consumer on the channel whose only job is that decision, and the decision can follow rules: this kind of message only to that performer, no more than one at a time each, a waiting message kept until its performer is free. Competing consumers racing for the next message could keep none of these, since none of them knows what the others hold. The price is that every message now passes through one place, and a message waiting for its performer waits there rather than in the channel.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public execution guide. In DotLn the operator moves a work order along with a short phrase: resume: next to have it implemented, resume: fix to have it repaired after a failed check, resume: verify to have it checked and resume: final review for its last review. The guide's table of roles gives next and fix to the executor, verify to the verifier and final review to the reviewer. Its router, which this study calls a dispatcher because a router is a different pattern in this book, consults only the order's recorded status, starts a new worker for the one phrase that status calls for, and checks the status again when that worker finishes, without reading the order or its changes. Picture one such dispatcher in front of requests about three orders, with a single executor, verifier and reviewer to share between them. It can send each request to the performer its kind of work names, which a pool of identical consumers could not do: whichever of them was free would take whatever request came next.

example.name: One dispatcher hands requests to the executor, verifier and reviewer
example.description: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public execution guide: requests about {orders} come down the Requests channel one at a time: i, to implement order 31, at frame 1; f, to fix order 30, at frame 3; r, to review order 29, at frame 5; and v, to verify order 31, at frame 8. The Dispatcher reads each request on the frame after it arrives and hands it to one of {performers} performers, one for each kind of work, each working on at most {inflightLimit} request at a time. Implementing order 31 takes the executor five frames from hand-over; the other three jobs are still under way when the example ends.

step0.title: Take each request off the channel
step0.text: The dispatcher is the Requests channel's only reader, so every request reaches it once, in the order it was sent; it reads each on the frame after it arrives. The channel itself knows nothing of performers.

step1.title: Choose the performer from the request
step1.text: It looks at the kind of work the request asks for and nothing else: implementing and fixing are the executor's, verifying is the verifier's and reviewing is the reviewer's.

step2.title: Hand it over, or keep it waiting
step2.text: If that performer is below its limit of {inflightLimit} request at a time, the dispatcher hands the request over at once. Otherwise the request waits in that performer's queue, in arrival order, even while the other performers are idle.

step3.title: Release the queue as performers finish
step3.text: When a performer finishes, the dispatcher hands it the oldest request waiting for it, if there is one. A request for another performer never waits behind it.

pseudocode.ordinary:
on each request from the Requests channel:
  (the dispatcher is the channel's only reader)

  performer = the one for the request's kind of work:
    implement or fix -> executor, verify -> verifier,
    review -> reviewer

  if performer is below its limit of requests in hand:
    hand the request to it
  else:
    add the request to the end of performer's queue

when a performer finishes a request:
  if its queue is not empty:
    hand it the oldest request in its queue

item1.relevance: Spring Integration, the Spring portfolio's messaging and integration framework, builds a dispatcher into its point-to-point channels; the reference guide's page on channel implementations describes it.
item1.explanation: A DirectChannel hands each message to one of its subscribed handlers through an internal message dispatcher, choosing by a load-balancing strategy, round robin or one you supply, and with failover, on by default, trying the next handler when one throws. An ExecutorChannel runs the same dispatch on a TaskExecutor, so a handler may run off the sender's thread and no transaction spans the two; a PartitionedChannel keeps every message with the same partition key on the same single thread, which preserves their order.

item2.relevance: Apache Pekko, an Apache Software Foundation project, builds programs from actors; its typed routers are themselves actors that pass each message on to one of a set of routee actors.
item2.explanation: A pool router spawns a set number of child routees from one behaviour and forwards each message to one of them, round robin by default; a group router finds its routees through the receptionist and by default picks one at random. With consistent hashing, a message's key decides its routee, and that choice holds only while no routee joins or leaves. The guide warns that the router is itself an actor with one mailbox, so it routes messages one at a time and can become the bottleneck under heavy load.

limits.item0: Specialised performers cannot help each other. While f waits for the executor, the verifier and the reviewer stand idle with nothing they may take, and the executor's queue clears only as fast as the executor works. When the work is interchangeable, a pool of identical performers, or competing consumers on the channel, keeps every performer busy; specialise only where performers really differ.
limits.item1: A waiting request has left the channel. f waits in the dispatcher's memory, where no other reader can see it and a crash would lose it, and concatMap's queue has no bound, so a burst of requests for one performer grows it without limit. If the channel is durable, take a request off it only when its performer is free, or bound the queue and decide what happens to the overflow.
limits.item2: The dispatcher knows kinds of work, not orders. A request to verify order 30 sent while the executor was still fixing order 30 would go straight to the idle verifier, which would check work not yet done. Order holds within one performer, since concatMap keeps arrival order, but not across performers, as r overtaking f shows. Where requests about one order must not overtake each other, key the performers by order, as Spring Integration's partitioned channel keys its threads.
limits.item3: Everything passes through one reader, so the dispatcher's own pace caps the throughput of every performer and its failure stops them all; Pekko's routing guide makes the same point about a router actor's single mailbox. When the dispatcher itself becomes the bottleneck, split the channel by kind of work instead.
limits.item4: The analogy departs from DotLn in two places: the guide's router follows a single order through its phases one after another, rather than serving a channel shared by several orders, and where another session already holds a worktree's writer reservation the guide refuses the second dispatch instead of keeping it waiting.

item0.why: When performers are interchangeable and each can take requests from the channel itself: there is no single dispatcher to slow or fail, though nobody can specialise or keep order per key.

item1.why: When each performer can filter the channel for its own kind of message, as Camel suggests with JMS selectors: the choice moves from a dispatcher into each consumer's selector.

item2.why: When each kind of work can have a channel of its own: the specialisation moves out of the dispatcher into the channel layout, and each performer's queue stays in its own channel.

item3.why: When the dispatcher should take a request only once a performer is free, leaving the queue in the channel rather than in its own memory.

item4.why: When the reader should act the moment a request is pushed to it rather than ask for one, as this dispatcher does; that is why the dispatcher must hold whatever it cannot hand over yet, where a polling consumer would leave it in the channel.

item5.why: When messages should go to different channels, each with its own consumers, rather than to performers inside one consumer.

The words in a box say what that box is doing or holding. A token is green while it moves and outlined while a box holds it, and a box a token leaves or reaches is outlined in green.

intuition.text: Expiration turns waiting into a decision. The sender says how long a message stays worth acting on, and the age is judged against that limit later, by whoever would hand the message on or read it, not when it was written. A message that is too old is set aside where someone can see it, instead of being acted on late and passing for current work.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public execution guide: there the operator starts a role's work with a short instruction the guide calls a dispatch, and every dispatch has limits on how long its work may run. Picture requests to verify orders queued for one verifier. A request that has waited too long would check work that may have moved on since, so it is better kept, unverified, in a dead letter record than run late. DotLn's domain model shows the same kind of judgement made by whoever reads: it treats a beacon, a status file whose size and modification time the platform reads as a signal, as stale once its age at the moment of reading reaches a set threshold, so the reader decides what is too old, not the writer.

example.name: Requests to verify, with a time limit
example.description: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public execution guide, where the operator, the person directing the work, starts each piece of work with one short instruction that the guide calls a dispatch. Here the operator sends three requests to a queue in front of one verifier: a, b and c ask for orders 31, 32 and 33 to be verified, and are sent at steps 1, 3 and 5. Each is worth starting only within {timeToLive} steps of being sent. The verifier receives a at step 2 and is busy with it until step 8, so b and c wait. When the verifier is free again, b is past its limit and goes to the dead letter channel instead; c is still within its limit and reaches the verifier at step 9.

step0.title: Set the limit as the request is sent
step0.text: Each request carries the step after which it is no longer worth starting: {timeToLive} steps after the operator sent it, however long anyone takes to look at it.

step1.title: Wait in line while the verifier is busy
step1.text: One verifier works on one request at a time. The others wait in the queue in the order they were sent, and their time runs out while they wait.

step2.title: Check the limit when a request's turn comes
step2.text: When the verifier is free, the queue looks at the oldest request. If its limit has passed, the request goes to the dead letter channel and never reaches the verifier, and the queue looks at the next one straight away.

step3.title: Hand on what is still fresh
step3.text: A request still within its limit reaches the verifier on the next step and keeps it busy until it is verified. Nothing checks the limit again once the verifier has it.

pseudocode.ordinary:
on each request from the operator:
  expires = now + time to live
  add the request, with its expiry, to the back of the queue

whenever the verifier is free and the queue is not empty:
  take the oldest request from the queue

  if now > its expiry:
    send it to the dead-letter channel
    (the verifier is still free: take the next one)

  otherwise:
    hand it to the verifier on the next step
    the verifier is busy until it has verified it

visual.textEquivalent: Step {step}: {moves}; {held}; {states}. The Request queue hands the Verifier only requests still within {timeToLive} steps of being sent, and moves older ones to the Dead letter channel.

item1.relevance: Apache Artemis is a message broker. Its user manual, at version 2.57.0 when read, documents expiry as a broker enforces it, which is where most systems put this pattern.
item1.explanation: A sender gives a message a time-to-live, through the JMS producer or as an absolute expiration time through the core API, and once that time has passed the broker no longer offers the message to consumers. An address can name an expiry address where expired messages are kept to be read later; without one they are dropped. Address settings can turn expiry off, supply a delay for messages that have none or hold delays within a range, expired messages can be given a limit of their own, and a reaper thread looks through the queues for expired messages, every thirty seconds unless configured otherwise.

limits.item0: Expiration decides which waiting request is lost; it does not shorten the wait. Raise the limit until b is still within it at step 8, and b holds the verifier for its whole verification while c, which arrived young, waits behind it and can expire in its place. When requests expire because one consumer cannot keep up, more consumers on the same channel help; tuning the limit only moves the loss.
limits.item1: The limit is checked only when the verifier is free, so an expired request sits in the queue until its turn comes and the dead letter channel learns of it late. Brokers that also sweep their queues, as Apache Artemis does every thirty seconds by default, narrow that gap; neither removes a message at the instant it expires.
limits.item2: An expiry time compares two clocks: the one that set it and the one that reads it. Skew makes a fresh message look stale or a stale one fresh, which is why Camel's page asks for clocks kept in step and why DotLn labels a beacon whose time lies after the reading as clock skew rather than fresh or stale. Setting and checking on one clock, the channel's own, as this example does, avoids skew, at the price of not counting the time a message took to reach the channel.
limits.item3: The limit governs waiting, not working: once the verifier has a request nothing checks the limit again, and a long verification overruns freely. Bounding the work needs a timeout on the work itself. Here the analogy breaks: DotLn bounds how long a running piece of work may take and refuses to start more until the operator accepts the overrun, and it refuses a second dispatch outright while another session holds the work, instead of queueing it, so a request there is refused rather than left waiting to expire.
limits.item4: A dead letter channel is only a record if someone reads it. Unread, it turns expiry into silent loss and grows without bound; Artemis, for one, can let expired messages expire in their turn, which trades the record for the space.

item0.why: Dead Letter Channel is where expired messages go here; read it when deciding who watches that channel and what happens to a message once it lands there.

item1.why: The expiration mechanics are the next question once the limit matters: an absolute expiry time or a time-to-live, skewed clocks, and replies that expire.

item2.why: Competing Consumers is the choice when messages expire because one consumer cannot keep up: several consumers on the channel shorten the wait instead of moving the loss.

item3.why: Request-Reply is where the late message is a reply: a requester that has stopped waiting needs its reply to expire too, or it acts on an answer nobody still wants.

item4.why: Guaranteed Delivery is the opposite pressure, keeping every message until it is acknowledged; reach for it when losing a message is worse than acting on it late, and pair the two when a kept message can outlive its use.

intuition.text: Keep a diary of the traffic without stopping it. Each time a record is handed on, a note about it is dropped into a box beside the road, and the hand-over carries on without waiting. Long after the records themselves have been used up and gone, questions about what happened are put to the box, never to the people doing the work. What the box can answer depends on what each note kept, and on every note arriving.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public domain model and its audit document: an order's records pass from the executor to the verifier and on to the reviewer, and each order also owns an append-only control segment in the control log, from which indexes and other views are rebuilt. Read that log, with its indexes, as this pattern's store: the hand-overs are the live flow and the log is the record of it. For each kind of record one then decides whether its entry keeps the whole record or only its envelope, much as the audit document's fidelity levels run from a short receipt up to complete event envelopes. Audit, in turn, reads the log and never the hand-overs in progress, as the document's audit projections are folds over the retained log.

example.name: The audit reads the control log after the work is done
example.description: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public domain model and audit document: the executor hands the evidence of orders 31 and 32 to the verifier, and the verifier files a report on each with the reviewer. Every hand-over also fires a copy at the control log, which keeps {keptInFull} in full and only the envelope of {envelopeOnly}. The audit questions the log about order 31 once the reviewer has finished with it, and later about order 32. The log is down for one hand-over.

step0.title: Fire a copy beside the work
step0.text: When a role sends a record on the work channel, it also sends a copy to the store on a channel of its own, and waits for no answer. The hand-over never depends on the copy arriving.

step1.title: Decide what each kind of copy keeps
step1.text: For each kind of record the copy keeps either the whole record or only its envelope: which record, on which channel, when. Here the log keeps {keptInFull} in full, because their verdicts answer later questions, and only the envelope of {envelopeOnly}, whose content stays with the roles.

step2.title: Keep what arrives
step2.text: The store appends each copy it receives and sends nothing back into the flow. A copy that arrives while the store is down is lost, and nobody in the flow is told.

step3.title: Answer from the store alone
step3.text: Questions about the flow go to the store, which can answer them after the records themselves have been consumed. An answer is only as complete as the copies that arrived: a lost copy looks the same as a record that was never sent.

pseudocode.ordinary:
when a role sends a record to the next role on the work channel:
  send the record on the work channel
  send copyOf(record) to the store on the copy channel, without waiting

copyOf(record):
  if record is a verification report: keep it whole
  otherwise: keep only its envelope (which record, which channel, which step)

when the store receives a copy:
  if the store is up: append the copy to its entries
  otherwise: the copy is lost, and no one is told

when the audit asks about an order:
  look up that order's entries in the store
  answer from those entries alone
  (a record whose copy was lost is simply missing)

visual.textEquivalent: At step {step}, {moves}. Work records travel between the roles, copies travel to the control log on a channel of their own, and the audit asks only the log. Now {states}; {held}.

item0.relevance: Spring Integration is the Spring portfolio's messaging and integration framework. Its reference has a Message Store page in its System Management part, and the name means something different there that a reader of Spring code will meet first.
item0.explanation: Spring Integration reads the pattern as durable buffering. Components that hold messages for a while, such as a QueueChannel or an aggregator, take a message-store attribute, so what they hold can survive a failure; behind one MessageStore interface sit an in-memory default and JDBC, Redis, MongoDB and Hazelcast stores. That is a store of messages still in flight rather than an archive of copies for reporting. The page is plain about what persistence costs: payloads and headers are serialised, the JDBC store by default drops headers that cannot be serialised, and a temporary reply channel carried in a header does not survive the trip through a persistent queue.

item1.relevance: NServiceBus is a .NET messaging framework from Particular Software. Its auditing feature is close to the pattern as the catalog draws it: copies of the traffic gathered in one place for later diagnosis.
item1.explanation: An endpoint set up to audit forwards a copy of every message it has processed successfully to a central audit queue, with added headers giving the processing start and end times, the host and the endpoint; a message that fails goes to the error queue instead and is not copied. ServiceControl reads the audit queue to serve the platform's diagnostic and visual tools. The page is frank about the costs: turning auditing on for every endpoint sends twice as many messages through the system, some message types can be left out with a custom pipeline behaviour, and an audit queue nobody drains can fill until no endpoint that audits into it can process messages.

item2.supports: In the platform every order has its own append-only control segment; one shared fold works out lifecycle legality and evidence separately for each order, and selection picks the order to look at; and each completion records who performed it, with the harness, model and effort used.

item3.title: DotLn · Audit, records, resilience, and privacy
item3.supports: The platform's audit document, in its Fidelity levels section, ranges from an M0 beacon and an L0 receipt up to L4 governed raw, which keeps the complete event envelopes, and warns that more fidelity is not better in itself, because every level serves its own readers under its own access and retention rules. Its Audit projections section builds the audit views by folding one kept JSONL log without reading or writing anything else, so they can be rebuilt at will, and its Persistence and recovery classes section treats the event log as the authoritative record and Markdown, dashboards and indexes as derived views that can be thrown away and rebuilt from it.

limits.item0: A copy fired and forgotten can be lost, and the flow never notices. When the log is down, the evidence of order 32 still reaches the verifier but its copy does not, so the audit later finds a passing report with nothing behind it, and from the log alone it cannot tell a lost copy from evidence that was never handed over. Where the store must be complete, send the copies with guaranteed delivery and pay for it in storage and acknowledgements, or reconcile the store against counts the flow keeps for itself.
limits.item1: Keeping only the envelope saves traffic and keeps sensitive content out of a second place, but some questions then have no answer: here the log can say that evidence 31 was handed over and never what it contained. Keeping every record whole doubles what is stored and copies whatever the records hold into a store with its own access and retention duties. DotLn's audit document makes the same point: more detail is not better in itself, since each level of detail serves its own readers under its own access and retention rules. When content is needed later but should not travel twice, a claim check keeps it once and passes a key.
limits.item2: The copies are not free. Each record sent becomes two messages, and if the store stops reading, its channel fills: NServiceBus's documentation warns that an audit queue nobody drains can grow until no endpoint auditing into it can process messages, so a stalled store can halt the very flow it was meant to leave alone. Size the copy channel, and watch the store's own backlog on the control bus.
limits.item3: The store sees only what crosses channels. It records that the executor handed evidence 31 to the verifier, not what the verifier did with it or whether it dropped it inside; a component's own decisions need its own reports, or a smart proxy or a pair of taps around it.
limits.item4: Here the analogy breaks: DotLn's control log is not a side copy. Each order's control segment is append-only, the shared fold derives the order's lifecycle legality from it, and indexes and Markdown views are projections rebuilt from that canonical log. Losing a message store leaves the flow running with a blind spot; losing DotLn's log would lose the order's recorded state. The platform's log is closer to an event-sourced record than to this pattern's archive, and a gap like this example's would be a defect there rather than an accepted cost.

item0.why: Reach for a wire tap when a channel's senders cannot be changed to send copies themselves: the tap copies every message on the channel to the store's channel and leaves the flow as it was.

item1.why: Use a message history when a message should carry its own path, for debugging it while it travels, with no central store and no extra channel.

item2.why: Read this comparison when choosing between history carried in the message, gone once the message is consumed, and a central store, which keeps everything but needs copies and storage.

item3.why: Use a claim check when the content itself must be kept for later but should not travel with every message or be stored twice: it is kept once and a key travels instead.

item4.why: The copy channel is management traffic: read the control bus for the separate channels it rides on, and for keeping watch on the store itself.

item5.why: Reach for guaranteed delivery on the copy channel when a lost copy is not acceptable, at the price of storing and acknowledging every copy at each hop.

example.caption: Each token is one message. e and r are the evidence and the verifier's report on order 31, and E and R the same records on order 32; they travel between the roles on the work channel. 1, 2, 3 and 4 are the copies of e, r, E and R, fired at the Control log on a channel of their own: 1 and 3 keep only an envelope saying which record went where and when, 2 and 4 the whole report. q and Q are the Audit's questions about orders 31 and 32, and a and A the log's answers. The Executor, the Verifier and the Reviewer are the roles doing the work; the Control log is the message store, keeping every copy that reaches it; the Audit is whoever questions the flow afterwards, and it asks only the log. The words in a box say what that box is doing, and the tokens in a box are the messages it holds. A token is green while it moves and outlined while a box holds it, and a box a token leaves or reaches is outlined in green.

start.note: Nothing has moved. The audit will learn about the work only from what reaches the control log.

0.note: The executor sends e, evidence 31, to the verifier and at the same moment fires 1, its envelope, at the control log: which record, on which channel, at which step. The hand-over does not wait for the log.

1.note: The verifier sends r, its report on order 31, to the reviewer and fires 2, a copy of the whole report, at the log. A report is short and its verdict matters later, so its copy keeps it all.

2.note: The reviewer finishes with r and lets it go. No role holds anything of order 31 any more; only the log's entries remain.

3.note: The audit sends q, a question about order 31, to the log. It asks the log, not the roles or the work channel.

4.note: The log sends back a: evidence 31 was handed over and report 31 passed. It cannot say what the evidence contained, because 1 kept only its envelope.

5.note: The log is down when the executor sends E, evidence 32, to the verifier. E arrives, but 3, its envelope, is lost, and nothing in the work notices.

6.note: The log is up again when the verifier sends R, its report on order 32, to the reviewer, so 4, the copy of R, is kept.

7.note: The audit sends Q, a question about order 32, to the log.

8.note: The log sends back A: report 32 passed, with no evidence behind it. E was handed over, so the gap is in the record and not in the work, but from the log alone the audit cannot tell a lost copy from evidence never sent.

intuition.text: A translator lets two parties keep their own formats. It stands on the channel between them, reads each message in the shape the sender writes, writes the same message in the shape the receiver reads, and then forgets it: it keeps no state, so one message in is one message out, at once and in order. The plumbing is the easy part, a single map in RxJS. The work is in the mapping: deciding what each field becomes, and what to write where the old shape has nothing to say.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against this app's catalog loader at its pinned commit. The catalog loads each book's rows as one bundle, a chunk, and accepts a chunk in the older tool-v0 shape or in tool-v1. Each tool-v0 row goes through a temporary compatibility reader that adds what tool-v1 expects: a definition saying the old catalog has none, and a verification marked partial because no reading of the source is available. Read as messaging, a legacy chunk is a sender that writes only tool-v0, the Tools home, the catalog's front page, is a receiver that reads only tool-v1, and the compatibility reader is the translator between them: neither end changes, and only the reader knows both shapes. DotLn's own documents describe the same move, read here as analogies too: a status page generated from an order's history, and one reviewed source rendered for different readers with its facts unchanged.

example.name: Three legacy rows read for the Tools home
example.description: As an analogy, read against this app's catalog loader: suppose a book's chunk were still in {from}. It holds three rows, {rows}, and sends one at each of frames 1, 2 and 3 before finishing at frame 4. The Tools home reads only {to}. The translator rebuilds each row in {to} in the frame it arrives: it keeps the id, marks the definition unavailable and the verification partial, and keeps nothing between rows.

parameters.rows: eip:60 Message Translator, eip:145 Normalizer and eip:146 Canonical Data Model

step0.title: Take one row as it was written
step0.text: The translator receives a row from the {from} channel. It knows the sender's shape and nothing else about the sender, and the sender knows nothing about the Tools home.

step1.title: Refuse a shape it does not know
step1.text: If the row is not in {from}, there is no mapping to apply, and a guess would hand the Tools home a row that looks right and is not. The translator stops with an error naming the shape. In this reading the error ends the stream; the limits say what to do when the other rows should still flow.

step2.title: Rebuild the row in the receiver's shape
step2.text: Keep what both shapes share, the row's id, and write the fields {to} adds. Where {from} has nothing to say, say so plainly: the definition is marked unavailable and the verification partial, never filled with something plausible.

step3.title: Send it on at once, keeping nothing
step3.text: The new row leaves on the {to} channel in the frame the old one arrived. Nothing is kept for the next row, so the translator never reorders, merges or holds rows back: one row in is one row out.

step4.title: Complete with the sender
step4.text: When the chunk completes, the translator completes the {to} channel. It has nothing left to flush, because it never held anything.

pseudocode.ordinary:
on each row from the tool-v0 channel:
  read its id and the shape it says it is in

  if the shape is not tool-v0:
    stop with an error naming the shape
    (no row after this one is translated)

  new row = the same id,
            shape tool-v1,
            definition marked unavailable,
            verification marked partial

  send new row on the tool-v1 channel now
  (nothing is remembered for the next row)

when the chunk completes:
  complete the tool-v1 channel

item0.relevance: Apache Camel is an open-source Java integration framework whose routes are assembled from the Enterprise Integration Patterns, and its documentation gives this pattern a page of its own.
item0.explanation: Camel offers several ways to translate a message on a route: a transform or set-body step with an expression, a processor or bean that converts the body in Java, and a templating component, Velocity in the page's example, that renders the new body from a template; data formats that marshal and unmarshal between encodings are a further way, which the page leaves to the Marshal page. Each worked example, shown in Java, XML and YAML, is a route that takes a message from one endpoint, converts it and passes it on, so the translator is one step on the route and the endpoints at either end never see each other's format.

item1.relevance: Spring Integration is the Spring portfolio's messaging framework. It implements this pattern as its transformer endpoint, documented on its own page, though the page does not use the pattern's name.
item1.explanation: A transformer sits between an input and an output channel and converts the payload, or the whole message, so a producer need not know what type the next consumer expects. It can be a plain method marked @Transformer, a transform step in the Java DSL or an XML element, and the framework ships ready-made ones for strings, maps, JSON, Java serialisation, Avro and Protocol Buffers. Two details stand out: a transformer may not return null, which raises a MessageTransformationException, and the page points a step whose result is optional to a service activator instead; and the page states that Spring Integration does not require a canonical data model or any particular format, leaving that choice to the application.

item2.relevance: Kafka Connect moves records between Apache Kafka and other systems through connectors, and its single message transformations are translators declared in a connector's configuration rather than written as code.
item2.explanation: The Kafka 4.1 user guide describes transformations as lightweight changes made one message at a time, listed as aliases in the order they apply. Its worked example wraps each line read from a file in a map with HoistField and then adds a static field naming the source with InsertField, so plain strings become structured records; other built-in transformations filter or rename fields, cast types, mask fields and convert timestamps, and predicates limit a transformation to the records that match.

limits.item0: A translator can only write what it can derive. Where {from} has nothing to say, an honest translator marks the gap, as this one marks the definition unavailable; one that fills it with a plausible default turns missing data into wrong data that looks right. If the receiver really needs the value, a Content Enricher that looks it up is the tool, not a cleverer mapping.
limits.item1: A record it cannot read is the hard case. In this reading the translator throws, and an error ends an RxJS stream, so rows$ stops at that record and every later row is lost, readable or not: had a row in tool-v2 arrived in place of n, the Tools home would have received only T, and c would never have been read. When the other rows should still flow, catch the failure for each record and send the bad one to an Invalid Message Channel; stopping, as the catalog loader does for a chunk of an unsupported shape, is right only when a partial answer would mislead.
limits.item2: The meaning has to survive the mapping. A translator that maps two different source values to the same target value loses the difference for good, and no later step can recover it. DotLn's publication rules guard against exactly this for implementation status labels, which must stay distinct in every edition however much else is adapted.
limits.item3: Translators between pairs multiply. Two formats need one translator each way; when several parties each keep a format of their own, the pairs grow with roughly the square of their number, and a canonical data model, with one translator in and one out for each party, becomes the cheaper thing to maintain.
limits.item4: Where the analogy breaks: the catalog loader upgrades a whole chunk at once inside one promise and reads the shape from the chunk rather than from each row, so the Tools home receives every row together when the chunk resolves. The rows' separate frames, and each row naming its own shape, are the messaging reading, not the loader's schedule.

item0.why: Reach for a Canonical Data Model when more than two parties each keep their own format: each then needs one translator in and one out, not one for every partner.

item1.why: A Content Enricher is the choice when the receiver needs data the sender never had: it looks the value up or computes it, where a translator can only mark the gap.

item2.why: A Normalizer is the choice when one kind of message arrives in several formats: it routes each to the translator for its format so that all of them come out in one.

item3.why: An Invalid Message Channel is where a message the translator cannot read should go when the other messages must keep flowing, instead of ending the stream.

item4.why: A Content Filter is the choice when the receiver needs less than the sender writes: it removes or flattens fields rather than rewriting the shape.

item5.why: A Channel Adapter is the choice when the other party is not on the messaging system at all; it connects the application, and translating its data remains a separate step.

intuition.text: A process manager is the one place that knows how far each run of a process has got. The steps never address each other: each answers the manager, and the manager reads that answer against everything it has recorded for the run before it picks the next step. Keeping that record in one place is what lets a route branch on a result, go round a loop and stop at a limit; it is also why every message has to pass through the manager.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public execution guide, in its section on the operator's resume phrases. An order passes from an executor, which builds it, to a verifier, which checks it, and on to a reviewer for a final review; a failed verification sends it back to the executor for repair before it is checked again. Each worker is started by a phrase, a short command such as resume: verify. When the operator types each phrase by hand, the operator is the manager, looking at the order's status and choosing what comes next. drive: WO-NNN hands that role to a router: it consults nothing but the order's status, starts a fresh worker for the single phrase that status calls for, and looks at status once more after that worker finishes. The order's progress is already kept in a record, its append-only log, rather than in anyone's head, so whoever reads that record can take the manager's place.

example.name: Driving one order through a repair loop
example.description: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public execution guide. The operator drives {order} at frame 1. Each worker reports to the router one frame after the phrase that started it, and the router sends its next phrase one frame after reading a report, so one message moves at each step: the executor builds the order, the first verification fails, the executor repairs it, the second verification passes and the final review passes. The router counts failed verifications against a limit of {failureLimit} and, after the final review, stops and asks the operator to merge. The reports are scripted at the frames a worker would finish; the router only ever sees them arrive.

step0.title: Start an instance on the trigger
step0.text: The drive names an order. A record of that order starts, with no step done and no failures, and the router sends the first phrase, resume: next, to the executor.

step1.title: Fold each report into the record
step1.text: Every report that reaches the router is folded into the order's record: which step has just finished and how many verifications have failed so far.

step2.title: Decide the next phrase from the record
step2.text: The record, not the report alone, picks the next step. The executor's reports that the order is built (implementation-ready) or repaired (repair-complete) both send it to the verifier; a passed verification sends it on to final review; a failed one sends it back to the executor for repair while fewer than {failureLimit} verifications have failed.

step3.title: Stop the route
step3.text: A passed final review ends the route, and so does a failed verification that reaches the limit of {failureLimit}. The router sends its stop to the operator and reads no more reports for this order.

pseudocode.ordinary:
on drive for an order:
  record = { order, failures: 0 }
  send resume: next to the executor

on each report for that order:
  update the record with the report
  if the report is a failed verification:
    record.failures = record.failures + 1

decide the next phrase from the record:
  implementation-ready or repair-complete: send resume: verify to the verifier
  failed verification, failures below the limit: send resume: fix to the executor
  passed verification: send resume: final review to the reviewer

if the final review passed, or failures reached the limit:
  send the stop to the operator
  read no more reports for this order
