item0.relevance: Apache Camel, the open-source Java integration framework, has a page for the pattern, and it answers by pointing to another of its patterns.
item0.explanation: Camel's page for the pattern says it builds a process manager from its Dynamic Router, which keeps track of how far the message has got and works out each next step as it goes. The Dynamic Router's own page, cited among the references, gives the mechanics: unlike a routing slip, which is worked out once at the start, the router's expression is evaluated again after every step until it returns null; one that never returns null keeps routing for ever; and state kept between evaluations belongs in the exchange's properties, so that concurrent messages do not share it. In Camel the record therefore travels with the exchange rather than sitting in a store of its own.

item1.relevance: Spring Integration, which brings these patterns to Spring applications, gives the pattern a page among its routers.
item1.explanation: It builds a process manager on its routing slip: the custom logic sits in a RoutingSlipRouteStrategy, which receives the request message and the previous step's reply and returns where the message goes next. Because the strategy may return any MessageChannel, including one created on the spot rather than declared as a bean, the next step can be chosen when nothing could have predicted it; the page's example returns a channel whose handler differs with the type of the payload.

item2.relevance: NServiceBus, Particular Software's service bus for .NET, calls its process managers sagas, and its page sets out what holding a long-running process's state involves.
item2.explanation: A saga is a message-driven state machine: a class with separately declared data that is persisted between messages. Named message types start an instance when no existing one matches, and every handled message is mapped to its instance through a correlation property such as the order's id. The page warns that messages can arrive out of order and that a saga not designed for that will discard some of them, and a handler marks the saga complete when the process is over.

item0.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns · Process Manager
item0.supports: The pattern's catalog entry, filed under Message Routing, describes the hub-and-spoke flow from a trigger message through each processing unit's reply back to the central unit, warns that the central unit can become a performance bottleneck and that using one for every problem is overkill, and names AWS Step Functions and GCP Workflows as the process managers of its serverless loan broker examples.

item1.title: Hohpe and Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns (Addison-Wesley, 2003) · Chapter 7: Message Routing, Process Manager
item1.supports: The book covers Process Manager in its chapter 7, Message Routing; the publisher's page lists that chapter in the book's contents.

item2.title: DotLn execution guide, pinned · Operator resume phrases — how you get dispatched
item2.supports: DotLn's execution guide describes drive: WO-NNN as handing an order to a router that consults only canonical status, starts a fresh worker for the phrase status calls for and rereads status afterwards, holding no writer; it lists, among the ends of a drive, the operator's merge, a third failed verification and a second failed final review; it has resume: fix repair the order and repair-complete recorded before the order is verified again; it computes status by folding the order's append-only event records; and it turns away a transition the lifecycle does not allow without writing anything.

item3.title: Apache Camel · Dynamic Router
item3.supports: Camel's Dynamic Router works out the next endpoint again after every step until its expression yields null, warns that an expression that never yields null makes it repeat without end, contrasts this with a routing slip computed once at the start, and advises keeping state between calls on the exchange for thread safety.

limits.item0: Every step depends on the manager. If its record of an order lived only in memory, a crash would forget how far every order had got; here the record is a fold of the order's log, so a fresh router can read it again, and a process manager without such a store needs one before it can be trusted with long processes. Every message also passes through it, so it is where load gathers.
limits.item1: A loop needs a bound counted in the record. Without the limit of {failureLimit} failed verifications, a verifier that never passes would keep the order cycling between fix and verify for ever; once {failureLimit} have failed, the next phrase is a stop, not another fix.
limits.item2: The manager has to match each report to its instance and to the step it is waiting for. Read without that check, a late or repeated report would set off a second dispatch. DotLn's lifecycle turns away a transition it does not allow without recording anything, so a stray report never reaches status; a process manager over plain messages makes the check itself, with a correlation identifier and its own note of the step in flight.
limits.item3: When the steps are known before the message sets out and never depend on results, a process manager is more machinery than the job needs: a routing slip or a fixed pipeline does the same without central state. Reach for the manager when results choose the route, as the failed verification does at frame 5.
limits.item4: The analogy breaks in two places. DotLn's router keeps no record of its own: it reads status afresh each time, so the state lives in the log and the decision in the router, where the pattern keeps both in one component. And one drive runs one order, one phase at a time, while a process manager usually runs many instances at once and may send work down parallel legs.

item0.why: A routing slip is the choice when the sequence of steps is fixed before the message sets out: the list travels with the message and no central record is needed.

item1.why: For the trade-off between the two directly: what each can express, and where each is cheaper to run and to change.

item2.why: A correlation identifier is what a manager running many orders at once needs to tell whose report has just arrived.

item3.why: For what the central record costs: the bottleneck, the single point of control, and recovering its state after a crash.

item4.why: An aggregator joins parallel legs: when a process sends work to several steps at once, it collects their answers before the manager decides.

flow.caption: The boxes: the Operator starts the route and is the only one who may merge; the Router is the process manager, which keeps its record of the order and decides each next step; the Executor builds and repairs the order, the Verifier checks it and the Reviewer gives it a final review. The workers never send to each other: every line runs to or from the Router. Each token is one message, and d is the operator's drive. Capitals are the router's phrases, each telling one worker to start: N resume: next (build), V resume: verify, F resume: fix (repair), R resume: final review, and M the stop that asks the operator to merge. Small letters are the workers' reports back: i implementation-ready, x a failed verification, c repair-complete, p a passed verification and a a passed final review. The words in a box say what that box is doing; in the Router they are its record: the step it calls for or awaits, and how many verifications have failed of the {{failureLimit}} allowed. A token is green while it moves, and a box a token leaves or reaches is outlined in green.

intuition.text: The channel does the copying, not the sender. The planner publishes each order once and never learns who is listening; the topic keeps a list of its subscribers and gives each one a copy of its own, so nothing one session does with its copy can reach another's. The list that counts is the one at the moment of publishing, and the topic keeps no copy afterwards: a session that subscribes later hears only what is published after it joins.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public architecture document. DotLn is the operator's agentic platform, where agent sessions take roles such as planning and execution on work orders, and the document describes feedback agents that listen to the platform's stream of events, each deciding from its own trigger when to act, off the main thread, sometimes dispatching actions in turn. Picture the planner, the role that files work orders, publishing each new order on an Order topic, and three agent sessions subscribed to it, each deciding by its own trigger what the order means for it. A board, or an audit listener on the log, could subscribe beside them: the planner would publish exactly as before and the three sessions would hear no less. The Competing Consumers study sends the same orders to the same sessions over a queue, so the two differ only in how the channel delivers.

example.name: Four orders on a topic with three sessions
example.description: The planner publishes orders {orders} on the Order topic at frames 1, 3, 5 and 7, and keeps publishing whether or not anyone listens. The topic has {subscribers} subscribers, Sessions 1, 2 and 3, all subscribed from frame 0 to the end, and hands out each order's copies one frame after it is published. The Competing Consumers study sends the same orders at the same frames to the same three sessions over a queue.

step0.title: Add a subscriber to the list
step0.text: When a session subscribes, the topic adds it to its list. From then on it is given a copy of every order published; it is given nothing published before, because nothing was kept.

step1.title: Copy each publication to everyone on the list
step1.text: When the planner publishes an order, the topic puts one copy on the line of each session on the list at that moment, and makes no copy for anyone else. The planner publishes once whatever the list holds, so adding a subscriber changes nothing for the planner.

step2.title: Each copy belongs to its subscriber
step2.text: A session reads the copy on its own line once, and reading it takes nothing from the other sessions' lines. A session that reads slowly falls behind on its own line only.

step3.title: Keep nothing
step3.text: Once the copies are handed out, the topic forgets the order: after each step that hands out copies it is empty again. A session that was not on the list when the order was published never hears of it.

pseudocode.ordinary:
when a session subscribes:
  add it to the list of subscribers
  (it is given only what is published from now on)

when the planner publishes an order:
  for each session on the list right now:
    put a copy of the order on that session's own line

when a session reads the copy on its line:
  take that copy off its line
  (no other session's copy is touched)

after the copies are handed out:
  forget the order
  (a session that subscribes later never hears of it)

Its example has one route send to a JMS topic and two further routes each consume from that same topic and pass what they receive to a different bean, so each bean is given every message the first route sends.

item1.relevance: Spring Integration is the Spring project's implementation of the book's messaging model inside a Spring application, with channels and endpoints as objects in the application context. Its PublishSubscribeChannel is an in-process topic.
item1.explanation: The channel hands every message it is sent to each handler subscribed to it, calling the handlers one after another; it cannot be polled, so a subscriber must itself be a handler. The page places it with event messages meant as notification, as against document messages that one handler processes. Since version 3.0 a send counts as successful when at least minSubscribers subscribers are present, and that minimum defaults to 0, so publishing to nobody is not an error unless it is raised.

item2.relevance: RabbitMQ is an open-source message broker. Its getting-started tutorials build small Node.js programs against it, and the third builds publish/subscribe as a logging system in which every running receiver gets every log message.
item2.explanation: A fanout exchange copies every message it receives to every queue bound to it. Each receiver declares its own exclusive queue with a name the server chooses and binds it to the exchange, so each subscriber has a line of its own, deleted when its connection closes. The tutorial notes that a message is lost when no queue is yet bound to the exchange, and accepts that because its receivers want only the messages flowing while they run.

In it, feedback agents listen to the stream of events and each decides from its own trigger when to act, working off the main thread and sometimes dispatching actions in turn. Files shared in the repository may carry messages at first, but canonical state lives in the append-only log.

limits.item0: A subscriber that is not listening misses what is published, and nothing tells it so. Had Session 3 subscribed at frame {lateJoin}, after the copies of order 33 went out, it would have received only order 34: the topic kept no copy of the first three for it. When a subscriber must catch up after joining late or being away, use a Durable Subscriber, for which the channel keeps publications while it is gone, or record every publication in a Message Store it can read back.
limits.item1: A copy for every subscriber is the wrong delivery for work that must be done once. If each session takes a new order as a job to start, all three start order 31, and every order is worked three times. Use a Point-to-Point Channel with Competing Consumers, which the companion study runs on these same orders and sessions, so each order goes to one session.
limits.item2: Publishing succeeds whether or not anyone hears it. A topic with no subscribers, or with subscribers whose triggers all ignore an order, accepts the order and nothing happens: Spring Integration's channel reports a send to nobody as a success unless a minimum number of subscribers is set, and RabbitMQ's fanout exchange drops a message no queue is bound to. A sender that must know its order was taken up needs a reply or a queue, not a topic.
limits.item3: Copies multiply with listeners. Each publication becomes one copy per subscriber, so every subscriber added adds traffic for every later order. A broker gives each subscriber a line of its own, so a slow one falls behind alone; the RxJS reading has no such lines, because share's Subject hands each value to its subscribers one after another in the same call, and a subscriber that blocks holds up the ones after it.
limits.item4: The analogy breaks at the log. DotLn's architecture keeps its canonical state in an append-only log, so a session that starts late could read the events it missed: the platform's stream is closer to a channel backed by a Message Store than to the bare topic drawn here, where order 31 is gone for good once its copies are handed out.

item0.why: Competing Consumers is the choice when the three sessions should share the orders out, each order to one of them, rather than each hear every one; the companion study runs these same orders over a queue.

item1.why: A Point-to-Point Channel is the choice when each message is meant for exactly one receiver, whichever it turns out to be.

item2.why: A Durable Subscriber is the choice when a subscriber that is away or joins late must still be given what was published meanwhile.

item3.why: A Message Store is the choice when a reader needs the history of what was published, not only what arrives from now on.

item4.why: A Wire Tap is the choice for watching one point-to-point channel's traffic without turning that channel into a topic.

item5.why: A Recipient List is the choice when the sender, not the receivers, must decide who gets each message, naming the recipients itself.

intuition.text: A recipient list works in two halves. First it decides, for this one message, who should have it; then it walks that list and hands each recipient its own copy. The list can change from one message to the next and can be empty, and it is worth keeping beside the message, because afterwards it is the only account of who was meant to receive what.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public execution guide. Once an order's release has been tagged and published, release close brings every declared export sibling, a separate repository kept in step with each release, up to date: it fast-forwards the sibling's main branch to one checked commit, tags that commit with the release's tag name, gives the sibling its own Release, and notes each refresh in its close record. A close that publishes nothing new, such as one for a target order whose change landed in another repository, or one for an older version, updates no sibling. So the list is worked out per release from two sources, the declared siblings, which are configuration, and the close itself, which is the message, and it is kept with the dispatch.

example.name: Three release closes and the declared siblings
example.description: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public execution guide. Siblings {declaredFirst} are declared at step 1, and three closes, {closes}, arrive at steps 2, 4 and 7. WO-240 publishes v0.95.0. WO-241 is a target order, whose change landed in another repository, and publishes no release. At step 6 a third sibling is declared, so the declared siblings become {declaredLater}, and WO-242 then publishes v0.96.0. The recipient list works out each close's list when the close arrives and, the step after, writes the order and the list to the close record and sends each sibling on the list its own copy of the close on that sibling's main branch; the closes end at step 8.

step0.title: Keep the declared siblings
step0.text: Each declaration replaces the siblings the recipient list knows. It is read when a close passes, so a change applies to later closes only.

step1.title: Compute the list for this close
step1.text: A close that publishes a release goes to every sibling declared at that moment; a close that publishes none, as WO-241 does, gets an empty list.

step2.title: Record the list with the dispatch
step2.text: Write the order and its recipients to the close record, an empty list included, so the record shows who was meant to have each release.

step3.title: Send each recipient its own copy
step3.text: Walk the list and send each sibling a fresh, unchanged copy of the close on that sibling's own channel. A sibling not on the list hears nothing.

step4.title: End with the closes
step4.text: When the closes end, every sibling's channel and the close record end with them.

pseudocode.ordinary:
on each declaration:
  declared = the siblings it names

on each close:
  if the close publishes a release:
    recipients = declared, as it stands now
  otherwise:
    recipients = nobody

  write (the close's order, recipients) to the close record

  for each sibling in recipients:
    send a fresh copy of the close on that sibling's main

when the closes end:
  end every sibling's channel and the close record

item0.relevance: Apache Camel is an open-source Java integration framework whose routes are assembled from the integration patterns by name. Its Recipient List EIP, built on its Multicast EIP, is documented here for the 4.22 long-term-support line.
item0.explanation: An expression computes the endpoints for each message: a constant for a fixed list, or a header the message carries for a dynamic one, as a comma-separated string or a collection. Camel sends to them one after another by default, or in parallel, and can aggregate the replies into a single message. When one recipient fails it carries on to the rest by default; with stopOnException it stops there, so the recipients after the failure get nothing. onPrepare can deep-clone each copy before it is sent, and ignoreInvalidEndpoints skips an endpoint that cannot be created.

item1.relevance: Spring Integration is the Spring portfolio's implementation of the integration patterns for Java applications. Its router implementations page describes the RecipientListRouter it ships.
item1.explanation: The router sends each message to a list of channels configured up front, and a selector expression per recipient, such as a test on the payload or on a header, decides whether that channel is on the list for a given message. Since version 4.1 recipients can be added and removed at run time through a control bus or JMX, so a router may start with none; a message no recipient takes goes to the default output channel if one is set, and otherwise raises a MessageDeliveryException. It also offers apply-sequence and ignore-send-failures settings.

item2.relevance: Apache Synapse is the Apache Software Foundation's mediation engine and enterprise service bus. RecipientListEndpoint.java, read at the Apache-Synapse-3.0.2 tag, is its recipient list.
item2.explanation: send takes its recipients from configured child endpoints, from cluster members, or from an expression evaluated on each message into a comma-separated list of addresses, keeping the endpoints it creates for those addresses in a small least-recently-used pool. For each recipient that is ready to send it clones the message context and stamps the clone with its position and the list's size, for an aggregator to use later. A recipient that is not ready is skipped, an expression that yields no address sends nothing, and a failing recipient is logged and reported as a failure.

item0.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns · Recipient List
item0.supports: For each message the pattern works out who should receive it and then delivers it on every one of those recipients' channels; the page describes this as two steps that implementations often merge, building the list and then walking it to send each recipient a copy, and says the content is normally left as it was.

item1.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns (Hohpe and Woolf, Addison-Wesley, 2003) · Chapter 7: Message Routing, Recipient List
item1.supports: The book covers the Recipient List in Chapter 7, Message Routing.

item2.title: DotLn execution guide · Workflow closeout and releases
item2.supports: Once a release's tag and Release exist, DotLn's release close brings every declared export sibling up to date: it fast-forwards the sibling's main branch to one commit it has checked, exporting the kit to it the first time, tags that commit with core's release tag name and gives the sibling a Release of its own. A close that publishes nothing new, whether for a target order or an older version, updates no sibling. The close record, release-close.json, and its summary note every refresh; a close is not finished while a refresh is blocked, a refused refresh is retried by running the same command again, and a retry that meets a sibling's existing tag and Release reports that sibling current.

limits.item0: There is no transaction across the recipients. Copies go out one by one, so when one recipient refuses, those before it already have the message and those after it may or may not, depending on whether the sender carries on or stops. A safe retry sends to the whole list again, so every recipient has to treat a copy it already holds as done. The guide's close does exactly this: a refused refresh blocks the close, and the retry reports an already refreshed sibling as current, an Idempotent Receiver at each sibling.
limits.item1: The list is computed when the message passes. Sibling C is declared at step 6 and receives nothing of v0.95.0, which went out at step 3; it hears only from WO-242 on. A recipient that must catch up needs the current state or a stored history, not the recipient list; the guide's refresh, for its part, can export the kit, the platform's shared files, to a sibling for the first time, which hands a new sibling the current state rather than the releases it missed.
limits.item2: An empty list has to be visible. WO-241 reaches nobody, which is right for a target order but looks the same, from any sibling, as a list computed wrongly. Recording every list with its dispatch, the empty ones included, is what lets someone check it afterwards.
limits.item3: In memory a copy is only as deep as you make it. The RxJS reading spreads each close into a new object for each sibling, so one sibling changing its copy cannot change another's, but anything nested inside would still be shared. A framework that sends real copies, such as Camel with onPrepare, settles this for you.
limits.item4: The sender has to know every recipient. When receivers should decide for themselves, a Publish-Subscribe Channel with a filter on each receiver needs no central list, at the cost of no single record of who was meant to receive what. When the copies are requests whose answers must be combined, the list is only the first half of a Scatter-Gather and needs an Aggregator after it.
limits.item5: The analogy breaks where the platform waits. DotLn's refresh is no fire-and-forget copy: each sibling gets its own commit and Release, checked before the push, and a close is done only when no refresh blocker remains. In the pattern the recipient list's work ends once each copy is on its channel; waiting until every recipient has finished, as the close does, is a further step the pattern leaves to whatever follows it.

item0.why: Reach for a Content-Based Router when each message has exactly one right destination, so no list is needed.

item1.why: Reach for a Publish-Subscribe Channel when every subscriber should get every message and the receivers, not the sender, decide who listens.

item2.why: Reach for Scatter-Gather when the recipients answer and their answers must be combined into one result.

item3.why: Reach for an Aggregator after the recipient list when its copies come back as replies that belong together.

item4.why: Reach for an Idempotent Receiver at each recipient whenever a failed dispatch is retried by sending to the whole list again.

item5.why: Read the robust-delivery trade-off for the two ways to make every recipient get its copy: send all the copies in one transaction, or let receivers ignore duplicates.

item6.why: Reach for a Dynamic Router when recipients should register and withdraw their own interest at run time instead of being written into one list.

intuition.text: A request and its reply are two separate messages, and nothing in messaging promises the second one. A function call always comes back, if only with an error; a request may be answered once, late, twice or never. So before it sends, a requestor has to settle how it will pick its work up again, how long it will wait, and what a reply that comes after it has stopped waiting means.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public domain model. DotLn is the operator's platform for running AI agents on pieces of work, and its kernel is the part that decides what happens next. When the kernel needs something done, it records a command with an id of its own, a commandId; an adapter picks the command up and hands it to a worker; the adapter's acknowledgement (a CommandReceipt) and later its result (a CommandResult) come back as events; and instead of blocking, the kernel keeps what remains to do once the result arrives as data it can resume from. The same pairing recurs whenever DotLn hands a piece of work to a worker: the worker's answer is a small result record, designed to answer the work it was given.

example.name: Two commands: one answered, one late
example.description: As an analogy, read against DotLn's domain model. The Kernel, the requestor, puts command {first} on the Outbox, the request channel. The Adapter, the replier, takes it, has a worker carry it out and puts the result on the Event log, the reply channel, and the Kernel takes the result and resumes the work it set aside. The Kernel then sends {second} and waits at most {timeoutSteps} steps. The Adapter sends back only a receipt saying the command was accepted, so the Kernel keeps waiting; when the deadline passes it gives up, and the result that arrives afterwards finds nothing waiting for it.

step0.title: Set the waiting work aside before sending
step0.text: Before the request leaves, the requestor decides how it will continue for each kind of reply, and how long it will wait. A reply can only reach a requestor that is already listening for it. Here the Kernel sets aside what to do with the result of {first} before sending it.

step1.title: Send on the request channel
step1.text: The request goes on a channel that carries requests to the replier and nothing back. The Outbox plays that part here; once the command is on it, the Kernel carries on instead of blocking.

step2.title: Answer on the reply channel
step2.text: The replier takes the request, does the work and writes on a second channel that leads back to the requestor. For {first} the Adapter writes the result; for {second} it first writes a receipt, which says only that the command was accepted.

step3.title: Resume on the reply, not on the receipt
step3.text: The requestor reads the reply channel. A receipt only says the request arrived, so it keeps waiting; the result is the reply, and the requestor resumes the work it set aside for that outcome.

step4.title: Give up at the deadline
step4.text: If no reply comes within {timeoutSteps} steps, as for {second}, the requestor stops waiting and takes its timeout path. A reply that turns up later finds nothing waiting, so it has to be recognised as late and must not be taken for the answer to anything else.

pseudocode.ordinary:
requestor, before asking:
  save what to do with each kind of reply
  set a deadline for the reply

requestor, to ask:
  put the request on the request channel
  carry on with other work; do not block

replier, for each request on the request channel:
  put a receipt on the reply channel (optional)
  do the work
  put the reply on the reply channel

requestor, for each message on the reply channel:
  if it is a receipt:
    note that the request was accepted and keep waiting
  if it is the reply to a request still awaited:
    clear the deadline
    continue with the saved work for that reply

requestor, when a deadline passes with no reply:
  stop waiting and take the timeout path
  a reply that arrives later is awaited by nobody: ignore it

item0.relevance: Apache Camel is an open-source integration framework built around these patterns. Its Request Reply page shows a framework turning the pattern into a property of each exchange rather than code the route writes.
item0.explanation: An exchange marked InOut tells the producing endpoint that the caller expects a reply. Over JMS the component then creates a temporary reply queue, sets JMSReplyTo and JMSCorrelationID on the request, sends it, matches the incoming reply to its request by the correlation id, since many exchanges may be waiting at once, and continues the route once the reply is on the exchange. With a component that already runs in the caller's thread, such as Direct, the pattern makes no practical difference.

item1.relevance: Spring Integration is the Spring portfolio's messaging framework. Its messaging gateway puts a request-reply exchange behind an ordinary Java interface, which makes the question of what a missing reply does impossible to ignore.
item1.explanation: Calling a gateway method sends a message on the request channel and waits on a temporary, anonymous point-to-point reply channel that the gateway puts in the message's replyChannel header. The page gives a whole section to replies that never come: a reply timeout bounds the wait and then returns null or throws, a reply produced after the method has returned still goes to a reply channel, and a method that returns a Future or a Mono makes the exchange asynchronous instead of blocking. A Mono sends nothing until something subscribes to it, so the listener is in place before the request leaves.

item2.relevance: NATS is an open-source messaging system. Its documentation builds request-reply out of plain publish-subscribe, so both channels stay visible.
item2.explanation: The client invents a private reply subject, an inbox, subscribes to it and publishes the request with that subject attached; the responder publishes its answer there. A client keeps one wildcard subscription for all its inboxes and routes each reply to the waiting request by the inbox's last token. Because replies are delivered at most once, every request carries a timeout; the server answers at once with a no-responders signal when nothing subscribes to the request subject; and a plain request keeps the first reply and silently discards any others.

item0.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns · Request-Reply
item0.supports: The pattern's public summary: a request and a reply each travel on a channel of their own, the reply channel is nearly always point-to-point, and the requestor either blocks for the reply or sets up a callback that a separate listener invokes when the reply arrives.

item2.title: DotLn · product document 02, Domain model, at commit 9139d91
item2.supports: The platform's kernel vocabulary: a Command carries a stable commandId; Invoke names a commandId, a command and a continuation for each result; Await waits for an event matching a commandId or correlationId and carries a timeout; a CommandReceipt acknowledges an accepted dispatch and a CommandResult is matched on payload.commandId; a continuation is the remaining program, stored as data so it can be resumed once the result is in; conditions are data, never closures; and the host returns only a small result envelope to the session that dispatched the work.

item3.title: DotLn · product document 03, Architecture, at commit 9139d91
item3.supports: The platform's outbox protocol: the kernel persists the command with its continuation, the adapter receives the persisted command, the result correlates by commandId and a command whose result never arrives stays pending and can be recovered; in its failure matrix, a result arriving after authority expiry is persisted but causes no state change.

limits.item0: A reply may never come, and the exchange itself never says so. A requestor that blocks with no deadline waits for ever, and one that saved its work keeps it for ever. Give every wait a deadline, as {second} has here, and decide beforehand what the timeout path does: retry, report or fail. NATS asks for a timeout on every request for the same reason.
limits.item1: A late reply still reports work that happened. The result for {second} arrives after the deadline, and the work did complete. Ignoring it is safe for a question; after a command with effects the requestor has to reconcile what the late reply says rather than assume nothing was done. DotLn's architecture keeps such evidence: a result that arrives after the permission its work ran under has expired is still recorded, though it changes nothing.
limits.item2: A receipt is not a reply. The receipt for {second} proves the command was accepted, and no result follows in time; a requestor that counted acceptance as success would mark the work done before anything was known. Keep the acknowledgement and the answer as different messages, as DotLn does with its CommandReceipt and CommandResult.
limits.item3: A reply channel that serves one request at a time needs no help. As soon as several requests are out at once, or several requestors share a replier, each reply has to say which request it answers and the replier has to be told where to send it; without that, a late reply such as the one for {second} can be taken for the answer to a newer request.
limits.item4: Blocking is the simpler requestor, but it ties up a thread and loses its place if the requestor crashes, while a callback has to restore the context it set aside. DotLn's kernel keeps what remains to do as data beside the command, a serialisable continuation, so it can resume after a restart, at the price of writing every condition as data rather than as a closure. When both sides are always up together and waiting costs nothing, a remote procedure call is simpler.
limits.item5: Where the analogy breaks: in DotLn the persisted command and its result are both recorded as events in the kernel's log, so the Outbox and the Event log here are two roles of one store rather than two separate pipes, and the kernel tells a result apart by its commandId rather than by the channel it came on.

item0.why: Reach for it as soon as more than one request can be outstanding. The request carries an id and the reply copies it back, so each reply says which request it answers: replies can then share one channel, and a late reply, like the result for cmd_2 here, is recognised as belonging to a request nobody awaits instead of being taken for the answer to a newer one.

item1.why: When several requestors share one replier, the request names the channel its reply should go to, so the replier needs no fixed reply channel.

item2.why: The trade-off this example settles on the callback side: what a blocked requestor costs and what a callback has to restore.

item3.why: When both sides are always up together and the caller can afford to block, a direct call is simpler; it hides the two channels, and with them the late or missing reply.

item4.why: When a request or a reply that has grown too old should be discarded by the messaging system, not merely ignored by the requestor after its own deadline.

item5.why: The request in this example is a command: a message asking the replier to do something rather than only to report.

start.note: The Kernel has a command, cmd_1, to send, and has set aside what it will do with each kind of result.

0.note: The Kernel puts command c, cmd_1, on the Outbox, the request channel, and carries on without blocking.

1.note: The Adapter takes c off the Outbox and has a worker carry it out.

2.note: The work is done, and the Adapter puts r, the result for cmd_1, on the Event log, the reply channel.

3.note: The Kernel takes r off the Event log and resumes the work it saved for a completed result. The request went out on one channel and the reply came back on the other.

4.note: The Kernel puts a second command, C, cmd_2, on the Outbox, and this time gives its wait a deadline.

5.note: The Adapter takes C off the Outbox and has a worker carry it out.

6.note: The Adapter puts A, a receipt saying cmd_2 was accepted, on the Event log.

7.note: The Kernel takes A off the Event log and keeps waiting: a receipt says the command arrived, not what came of it.

8.note: Nothing arrives on the Event log: the worker on cmd_2 is slow, and the Kernel goes on waiting.

9.note: The deadline passes with no result for cmd_2, so the Kernel stops waiting and takes its timeout path instead of hanging.

10.note: The work on cmd_2 finishes after all, and the Adapter puts R, its result, on the Event log.

11.note: The Kernel takes R off the Event log. It names cmd_2, which nothing waits for any more, so it changes nothing.

example.caption: Each token is one message. Lower-case letters belong to the first command, cmd_1, and capitals to the second, cmd_2: c and C are the commands, A is a receipt saying cmd_2 was accepted, and r and R are the results. The Kernel is the requestor: it sends commands and waits for their results. The Outbox is the request channel, which carries commands to the Adapter; the Adapter is the replier, which has a worker carry out each command; the Event log is the reply channel, which carries receipts and results back to the Kernel. The words in a box say what that box is doing. A token is green while it moves and outlined while a box holds it, and a box a token leaves or reaches is outlined in green.

intuition.text: Messages come in any order and leave in their proper one. A resequencer is a turnstile that knows the next number: the expected message walks straight through, an early one waits beside the gate, and when the missing one arrives, everything queued behind it walks through in a row. Read reactively, it is a scan over the next expected number and a buffer, flattened so that each arrival lets out nothing, one event or a whole run of events.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public domain model and architecture. A projection, such as a generated view of a log, has to apply the log's events in the order they were appended: a projection that applied a command's result before the command's persist would hold a result for a command it has not yet seen. DotLn numbers each log's events at the append boundary, evt_1, evt_2 and so on, which is exactly what a resequencer needs. Wherever those events travel by a route that loses order (writers that raced, a shared-file bus, or workers dispatched in order whose returns come back in any order before a consumer that must take them in sequence), the numbers let a resequencer put them back before the projection sees them.

example.name: A log's events over a bus that loses their order
example.description: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public domain model, whose append boundary numbers every event of a log. Here a log of {events} events, two commands each persisted, accepted by the transport with a receipt and answered with a result, reaches a projection over a bus that does not keep its order, such as the shared files DotLn's architecture accepts as a first bus. They come off the bus as evt_1, evt_3, evt_2, evt_5, evt_6 and evt_4. The resequencer expects evt_{nextSequence} first and holds each event that comes early; in the step after it sees an unbroken run from the number it expects, it sends that run down a first-in, first-out channel (FIFO in the drawing) to the projection, without changing the events.

step0.title: Know the next number
step0.text: The resequencer keeps one number, the next event the projection needs, starting at evt_{nextSequence}, and a buffer for anything that turns up early. Nothing else about the log is needed, but the events must carry those numbers.

step1.title: Hold an event that comes early
step1.text: An event whose number is not the expected one goes into the buffer and nothing is sent. evt_3 waits this way while evt_2 is missing, and evt_5 and evt_6 wait for evt_4.

step2.title: Pass the expected event on
step2.text: An event with the expected number goes down the FIFO channel in the next step, unchanged, and the expected number moves up by one.

step3.title: Release what the gap held back
step3.text: Each time the expected number moves up, the buffer is searched for the new one, and the whole unbroken run goes out together, in order: evt_2's arrival lets evt_3 out with it, and evt_4's lets out evt_5 and evt_6. The channel after the resequencer must keep that order, or the work is undone.

pseudocode.ordinary:
next = 1, the number of the first event the projection needs
held = an empty buffer
on each event from the bus:

  if the event's number is not next:
    put it in held, and wait for the next event

  in the next step, send it down the FIFO channel
  next = next + 1

  while held has the event numbered next:
    take that event out of held and send it down the FIFO channel after the last
    next = next + 1

visual.textEquivalent: Step {step}: {moves}; {held}; {states}. Events come off the bus in any order; the resequencer, expecting evt_{nextSequence} first, sends down the FIFO channel to the projection, one step after it sees it, only the unbroken run that starts at the number it expects.

item0.relevance: Apache Camel is an open-source Java integration framework whose routes are written in the vocabulary of these patterns. Its Resequence page offers two different algorithms under the one name, which shows that the pattern is a family of choices.
item0.explanation: An expression, typically a header holding a sequence number, gives each exchange its place. Batch mode, the default, collects exchanges up to a size or a timeout (100 messages or one second unless configured), sorts the batch and sends it on. Stream mode works on integer numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on and sends each exchange as soon as its predecessor has gone, keeping the rest in a backlog of 1000 by default; its timeout makes it give up on a missing number and move to the next, and the page relates the timeout to the largest delay between neighbouring messages. By default only the last of two exchanges with the same number is kept, and rejectOld throws MessageRejectedException for an exchange older than the last one delivered.

item1.relevance: Spring Integration is the Spring portfolio's messaging framework: it implements these patterns as message handlers between channels inside a Spring application. Its resequencer is built on the same correlating machinery as its aggregator.
item1.explanation: It stores messages in groups by their CORRELATION_ID header, as the aggregator does, but passes them on unchanged, in the order of their SEQUENCE_NUMBER header. By default it waits for the whole group that the SEQUENCE_SIZE header promises; release-partial-sequences sends each in-order run as soon as it is available. A group timeout can expire a group with a hole in it, either discarding its messages or, with send-partial-result-on-expiry, sending what it has in order, and messages that arrive for an expired group are discarded by default. The page says the resequencer is meant for short sequences with small gaps and warns of poor performance with many disjoint sequences full of gaps.

item2.relevance: Apache NiFi is a dataflow system that moves FlowFiles between processors arranged on a canvas. EnforceOrder is its processor for putting FlowFiles back into their original order after branches and error handling have scrambled them.
item2.explanation: A Group Identifier sorts FlowFiles into ordering groups, an Order Attribute gives each an integer and Initial Order says where a group starts. A FlowFile with the expected number goes to the success relationship and one with a later number to the wait relationship; after Wait Timeout a waiting FlowFile goes to overtook, passing the ones it was waiting for, and a FlowFile older than the current number goes to skipped. The page insists on NiFi's FirstInFirstOutPrioritizer for every downstream relationship until the order is fixed, which is the order-preserving output channel the pattern relies on.

item0.supports: The pattern catalog's page for the Resequencer: messages that took different routes can reach a later step out of order, the resequencer keeps the out-of-sequence ones in a buffer until the sequence is complete and publishes them in order, usually without altering them, and its output channel must preserve order.

item1.title: Hohpe and Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns (Addison-Wesley, 2003) · Chapter 7: Message Routing · Resequencer
item1.supports: The publisher's page for the book by Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, whose chapter 7, Message Routing, covers the Resequencer.

item2.title: DotLn domain model
item2.supports: In DotLn the append boundary assigns each event's eventId as evt_n, monotonic per log; CommandPersisted, CommandResult and CommandRefused are the outbox's event types and a CommandReceipt is the transport's acknowledgement; replay holds on to a result that comes before its persist and finishes the command once that persist record turns up; and the beacon fold reads the log in append order.

item3.title: DotLn architecture · The agentic communication core
item3.supports: DotLn's architecture accepts shared files in the repository as a first bus but never as canonical state; the append-only log is canonical, because of lost-update and ordering hazards.

limits.item0: A gap that never fills stops the projection for good. Lose evt_4 on the bus and evt_5 and evt_6 are never sent: the projection stays at evt_3, every later event of the log queues behind them, and the buffer grows without bound while nothing reports a fault. A resequencer needs a rule for a gap: wait a bounded time and then skip the number, as Camel's stream mode does, or route the overtaking events elsewhere, as NiFi's overtook relationship does; here the better rule is to fetch the missing event again by its number, since the log still has it.
limits.item1: A redelivered event is never let go. A bus that can deliver twice may bring evt_3 again after it has gone out. Its number is below the expected one, so this resequencer neither sends it again nor drops it: it stays in the buffer for good. Drop or report a number below the expected one, as NiFi's skipped relationship and Camel's rejectOld do, and keep the projection idempotent on eventId.
limits.item2: It can only restore the order its numbers record. DotLn's domain model meets a case a resequencer cannot mend: when a log presents a command's result before its persist, replay holds on to the early result and finishes the command once its persist record turns up, matching the two by commandId. The log's own numbers already put the result first, so ordering by them keeps the wrong order.
limits.item3: Everything behind a gap waits, even events the projection could use at once: one slow event delays all that follow it. Where the consumer does not care about order, such as a count of events by type, resequencing only adds delay and memory.
limits.item4: Numbers belong to a sequence. Each DotLn log numbers its own events, so a resequencer that serves several logs needs one expected number and one buffer per log, as Spring Integration keeps one per correlation id and NiFi one per group identifier; one counter shared by two logs would pass whichever log's evt_2 arrived first and hold the other's for good.
limits.item5: The analogy breaks where DotLn keeps order instead of restoring it. Its architecture treats shared files as no more than a first bus and keeps the append-only log as the source of truth, and a fold such as its beacon fold reads that log in append order, so nothing reaches it out of order. Reading the log directly is the cheaper fix; a resequencer is the repair for a channel that has already lost the order.

item0.why: Message Sequence is where the numbers come from: reach for it first, since a resequencer can do nothing for messages that do not say where they stand.

item1.why: Read the row on sequence numbering requirements for what the numbers must be: one numbering per sequence, without gaps, with a known first number.

item2.why: Competing Consumers is the most common reason order is lost: parallel consumers finish in any order, and a resequencer is what restores it if a later step needs it.

item3.why: An Idempotent Receiver answers the redelivery limit: a receiver that ignores an eventId it has already applied makes a duplicate harmless downstream.

item4.why: Choose an Aggregator when the related messages should become one message rather than all pass through in order.

notes.0: The Projection needs evt_1 first. No event has come off the Bus, and the Resequencer holds nothing.
notes.1: The Bus delivers evt_1, a CommandPersisted. It is the number the Resequencer expects, so it goes on in the next step.
notes.2: The Resequencer sends evt_1 on to the Projection and now expects evt_2.
notes.3: The Bus delivers evt_3, a CommandResult, before evt_2. Sending it on would show the Projection a result before the receipt that comes ahead of it, so the Resequencer holds it back.
notes.4: The Bus delivers evt_2, the CommandReceipt, and the gap before evt_3 is filled.
notes.5: The Resequencer sends evt_2 and then evt_3 on to the Projection, in order, and now expects evt_4.
notes.6: The Bus delivers evt_5 while evt_4 is still missing, so the Resequencer holds it.
notes.7: The Bus delivers evt_6, and the Resequencer holds it too: one missing event holds back {{held}} events that follow it.
notes.8: The Bus delivers evt_4, the second CommandPersisted, last. The run from evt_4 to evt_6 is now unbroken.
notes.9: The Resequencer sends evt_4, evt_5 and evt_6 on in order, and the Projection has the whole log.

example.caption: Time runs in frames, one event to a frame. bus$ is the order the events come off the bus, each digit an event's number in its log; inOrder$ is what the resequencer sends on to the projection, in log order, one frame after it sees an unbroken run.

flow.caption: Each token is one event of the log, with its number: 3 is evt_3. The events themselves are not changed, only their order. The Bus is the channel they travel over, and it does not keep their order. The Resequencer holds any event that comes early and, one step after it sees an unbroken run from the number it expects, sends that run down the FIFO channel, which keeps the order. The Projection is the view of the log that must take the events in order. The words in a box say what that box expects or holds. A token is green while it moves and outlined while a box holds it, and a box a token leaves or reaches is outlined in green; where several tokens do not fit apart, one capsule names them all.

intuition.text: Treat everything a worker does with the messaging system between begin and commit as a draft that only commit publishes. A crash in the middle then costs nothing on the channels: the message it took is still there to be taken again, and nothing half-sent has escaped to a reader. The draft holds only what the messaging system controls, though. Work done anywhere else in the meantime is real as soon as it is done, and that is where the duplicates of a retried transaction come from.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public architecture document, in its section on session lifecycle and resilience: a pending command waits in an outbox, a worker carries it out, a receipt of the result is published under the command's id, and a result entry, which DotLn calls CommandResult, is appended to the event log. A receipt and its log entry ought to commit together or not at all, and taking the command ought to be undone if the worker dies before both are done. The document describes DotLn reaching that end another way. The receipt goes out first; if the host crashes before the log entry is written, the command stays pending and recovery looks the receipt up. And each worker holds a five-second lease: when it runs out, the command is kept for a new attempt. That lease plays the part a visibility timeout plays for a cloud queue, the delay after which an unfinished message is offered again, since nothing commits the receipt and the log entry as one.

example.name: One command, a crash, a retry and a commit
example.description: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public architecture document. Command {command} waits in the outbox. The worker takes it inside a transaction, makes one write to a store the transaction does not cover, stages its receipt and its result entry, and crashes before committing. A fresh attempt, the last of {attempts}, does the same and commits, so the receipt and the result entry appear and the command leaves the outbox at one step, while the outside store has been written once per attempt.

step0.title: Open a transaction and receive
step0.text: The worker begins a transaction and takes command {command} from the outbox. The outbox stops offering the command to other workers but keeps it, because a receive inside a transaction can still be undone.

step1.title: Work outside the transaction
step1.text: Anything the worker does that the messaging system does not control, such as a write to another store, happens now and for real. The transaction has no way to take it back.

step2.title: Stage the sends
step2.text: The receipt and the result entry go into the transaction, not onto their channels. A reader of Receipts or Event log sees neither of them yet.

step3.title: Roll back on failure
step3.text: If the worker crashes or gives up before committing, the messaging system discards the staged sends and makes command {command} visible in the outbox again, ready for another attempt.

step4.title: Commit
step4.text: Commit is the single moment at which the receive and both sends become real: the command leaves the outbox in the same step as the receipt and the result entry appear.

pseudocode.ordinary:
transaction = begin()
command = receive from outbox within transaction
  (hidden from other workers, still in the outbox)

write to the outside store
  (not part of the transaction: done now, whatever happens next)

send receipt for command to receipts within transaction
send result entry for command to event log within transaction
  (staged: neither channel shows them yet)

on a crash or an error before commit:
  rollback(transaction)
  (staged sends discarded; command visible in the outbox again)

commit(transaction)
  (command removed, receipt and result entry visible, all at once)

item0.relevance: Apache Camel is an open-source Java integration framework whose routes are assembled from these patterns. Its page for the pattern shows how a route opts in to a transaction and what that takes underneath.
item0.explanation: A route becomes transactional when it is marked transacted straight after the endpoint it consumes from; Camel then finds a Spring or JTA transaction manager instead of implementing one of its own, and its JMS and SQL components take part. The page separates local transactions over one resource, such as a single broker, from global ones that span a broker and a database and need an XA-capable transaction manager, with the resources themselves set up for it. It also shows propagation policies, such as an audit insert in a transaction of its own that can commit while the main one rolls back, and advises using as few of them as possible.

item1.relevance: Spring Integration brings these patterns to Spring applications as channels and endpoints. Its transaction support page says which parts of a message flow a transaction covers.
item1.explanation: A flow started by a caller simply joins Spring's ordinary transaction management. A poller is the special case: it can put its receive inside the transaction, so a failed task rolls the receive back. Because the transaction is bound to the thread, handing a message to a pollable or executor channel ends it and commits even if a later step fails, unless that hand-off is itself transactional, such as a queue backed by a transactional message store or by JMS. Transaction synchronisation attaches actions to commit and rollback, such as moving a polled file to a success or a failure directory, and a pseudo-transaction manager offers those hooks where no real transaction exists.

item2.relevance: NServiceBus is Particular Software's service bus for .NET. Its transport transactions page sets out the guarantee levels under which a message handler can run, and one of them is this pattern in all but name.
item2.explanation: An endpoint picks one of four modes, limited by what its transport supports. Under sends atomic with receive, the incoming message and every message the handler sends commit or roll back together, so a handler that fails puts its message back on the queue with nothing sent; database work in the handler stays outside that transaction. Receive only keeps the message until an attempt succeeds but can leave ghost messages and zombie records, so handlers must be idempotent. The page's table shows Amazon SQS and RabbitMQ offering only receive-level transactions, and it recommends an outbox stored with the business data for exactly-once processing without a distributed transaction.

item0.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns · Transactional Client
item0.supports: The pattern's catalog entry, filed under Messaging Endpoints, gives its problem and solution and adds a cloud example: Amazon SQS does not offer transactional clients but hides a consumed message from other consumers until the consumer deletes it, making it visible again when a timeout expires.

item1.title: Hohpe and Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns (Addison-Wesley, 2003) · Chapter 10: Messaging Endpoints, Transactional Client
item1.supports: The book covers Transactional Client in its chapter 10, Messaging Endpoints; the publisher's page lists that chapter in the book's contents.

item2.title: DotLn product architecture, pinned · Session lifecycle & resilience
item2.supports: DotLn's architecture describes an outbox protocol in which each command is stored before an adapter picks it up and results are matched to commands by id; an inspection host that publishes each finished result as a receipt, never rewritten, filed under its command's id, and that, if it crashes between publishing a receipt and appending CommandResult, leaves the command pending for recovery to look the receipt up; five-second worker leases after whose expiry the command is kept for a fresh attempt; and it disclaims exactly-once effects on writes outside its store.

limits.item0: A transaction covers only what the messaging system controls. The write to the outside store happened before the crash and again on the retry, once for each of {attempts} attempts at command {command}. Make that write harmless to repeat, keyed by the command, or move it into the same store and transaction as the messages and publish it after commit, which is what an outbox does.
limits.item1: A command that fails every time is rolled back every time and comes straight back to the outbox: a poison message that keeps a worker busy for ever. The messaging system needs a redelivery count that moves such a message to a dead letter channel after a few attempts.
limits.item2: A request and the reply to it cannot share one transaction. The request is not sent until commit, so a client that waits for the reply inside the same transaction waits for ever. Commit the request in one transaction and receive the reply in the next.
limits.item3: Keep transactions short. Until commit or rollback the message taken is invisible to every other worker, so on a queue that must keep its order nothing behind it moves while one long transaction stays open.
limits.item4: Spanning the broker and another resource, such as a database, needs a distributed two-phase commit, which is slow and often unavailable, cloud queues included. Their substitute, a visibility timeout or a lease, returns the message only after the timeout and undoes nothing already sent, so delivery becomes at least once and the receiver must tolerate duplicates.
limits.item5: The analogy breaks where DotLn has no transaction at all. Its record describes the receipt being published before the result entry is appended, with recovery reconciling the two after a crash, and leases bringing a command back after its worker vanishes: reconciliation after the fact, not one commit.

item0.why: Reach for an idempotent receiver when an effect cannot join the transaction, as the outside write here cannot: make doing it twice harmless instead of trying to prevent it.

item1.why: Guaranteed delivery answers a different crash, the messaging system's own: persistence keeps the message, while a transaction decides when it counts as received.

item2.why: Competing consumers is the usual setting for this pattern: several workers on one queue, where a transactional receive is what lets a dying worker's message go back to the others.

item3.why: For the shapes a transaction bounds well, such as a receive with its sends or a receive with a database update, and why a request and its reply cannot share one.

item4.why: A dead letter channel is where a message that keeps rolling back should end up, instead of returning to the queue for ever.

example.caption: The boxes: the Outbox is the channel where command 7 waits to be taken; the Worker is the transactional client, which takes the command, works on it and sends inside a transaction; Receipts and Event log are the two channels it sends to; the Outside store is a store that no transaction covers. Each token is one message: c is command 7, r its receipt, e its result entry for the event log, and 1 and 2 the outside writes made by attempts 1 and 2. While a transaction is open, c shows in two boxes: the Worker has taken it, and the Outbox still keeps it, hidden from other workers, until the Worker commits. Tokens inside the Worker are staged in its open transaction and are on no channel yet. The words in a box say what that box is doing or holding. A token is green while it moves and outlined while a box holds it, and a box a token leaves or reaches is outlined in green.

start.note: Command 7 waits in the Outbox, where any worker could take it. Nothing has been taken, and Receipts, Event log and the Outside store are empty.

0.note: The Worker opens transaction 1 and takes c, command 7, from the Outbox. The Outbox hides the command from other workers but keeps it, because the take is not final until the Worker commits.

1.note: The Worker sends write 1 to the Outside store. No transaction covers that store, so the write takes effect at once, whatever later happens to transaction 1.

states.worker: r and e staged in transaction 1

2.note: The Worker sends r, its receipt, and e, its result entry, inside transaction 1. Both wait inside the Worker, staged, so Receipts and Event log are still empty.

3.note: The Worker crashes before committing, so transaction 1 rolls back: the staged r and e are thrown away and command 7 can be taken from the Outbox again. Write 1 is not undone.

4.note: A fresh attempt opens transaction 2 and takes c from the Outbox again. Nothing on the channels says that attempt 1 has already written to the Outside store.

5.note: The Worker sends write 2 to the Outside store: the same command has now been written there {{writes}} times, a duplicate that no rollback could prevent.

states.worker: r and e staged in transaction 2

6.note: The Worker stages r and e again, in transaction 2. Receipts and Event log are still empty.

7.note: The Worker commits. At that one step r reaches Receipts, e reaches Event log and command 7 leaves the Outbox, so no reader sees one without the others.
